bank.definition: A relatively permanent change in behavior or knowledge arising from practice or experience
bank.hint: Focus on how practice or experience changes the organism.
bank.scenario: Repeated practice changes the way a student performs a laboratory procedure.

bank.definition: Changes in an organism's mental representation of its environment because of experience
bank.hint: Ask whether something can be learned without an immediate visible response.
bank.scenario: A rat forms an internal map of a maze and later takes an unfamiliar shortcut.

bank.definition: Learning by observing others' behavior or hearing about their experiences
bank.hint: Think about whether direct personal consequences are necessary.
bank.scenario: A child avoids touching a hot pan after watching another child get burned.

bank.definition: A diminishing response to a frequently repeated stimulus
bank.hint: Focus on how response strength changes when an unchanged stimulus repeats.
bank.scenario: A student gradually stops noticing a steady background hum.

bank.definition: A previously neutral stimulus gains the ability to elicit a response after association with another stimulus
bank.hint: Consider automatic responses and associations between events.
bank.scenario: After repeatedly hearing a tone before food, a dog salivates to the tone alone.

bank.definition: A stimulus that evokes a response without prior conditioning
bank.hint: Identify what naturally triggers the reflex before training.
bank.scenario: Meat powder naturally produces salivation in Pavlov's dog.

bank.definition: An unlearned response elicited by an unconditioned stimulus
bank.hint: Look for a response that already occurs before the pairing.
bank.scenario: A dog salivates automatically when meat powder reaches its tongue.

bank.definition: A stimulus that initially does not elicit the target reflex before conditioning
bank.hint: Ask whether the cue originally predicts or produces the target reaction.
bank.scenario: Before training, a bell does not cause a dog to salivate.

bank.definition: A formerly neutral stimulus that elicits a learned response after being paired with another stimulus
bank.hint: Consider how the role of the cue changes after training.
bank.scenario: After several food pairings, the bell alone makes the dog salivate.

bank.definition: The learned response evoked by the conditioned stimulus
bank.hint: Identify the response specifically when the learned cue is given alone.
bank.scenario: A dog salivates to a bell even when no food is presented.

bank.definition: The initial strengthening of a conditioned response during stimulus pairings
bank.hint: Consider what happens across the first training trials.
bank.scenario: Salivation to a tone rises after several tone-and-food pairings.

bank.definition: A conditioned response weakens when the conditioned stimulus is presented without the unconditioned stimulus
bank.hint: Ask what changes when the expected event no longer follows a cue.
bank.scenario: A bell is sounded repeatedly without food until salivation fades.

bank.definition: An extinguished conditioned response temporarily reappears after time passes
bank.hint: Think about what can happen after a rest period following extinction.
bank.scenario: A dog again salivates to a bell after a day without training.

bank.definition: A conditioned response also occurs to stimuli resembling the original conditioned stimulus
bank.hint: Consider whether the organism treats similar cues alike.
bank.scenario: A dog trained to a circle also salivates to a similar ellipse.

bank.definition: Learning to respond differently to a conditioned stimulus and similar cues not forecasting the same event
bank.hint: Ask whether similar-looking cues have different consequences.
bank.scenario: A dog salivates to a circle but not an ellipse because only circles predict food.

bank.definition: A new neutral stimulus becomes conditioned through repeated pairing with an already conditioned stimulus
bank.hint: Ask whether the new cue is paired with food or with an existing learned cue.
bank.scenario: A light paired with a food-predicting tone eventually triggers salivation by itself.

bank.definition: A learned avoidance of a food or flavor associated with nausea, sometimes after one delayed pairing
bank.hint: Remember that biological preparedness can allow learning after a single event.
bank.scenario: A child avoids popcorn for months after a nauseating popcorn meal.

bank.definition: An inherited readiness to learn certain associations more readily because of their adaptive value
bank.hint: Consider whether all stimulus combinations are equally easy to learn.
bank.scenario: Rats learn to link nausea with taste more easily than nausea with light.

bank.definition: A rat study showing that nausea is associated preferentially with taste whereas shock is associated with audiovisual cues
bank.hint: Compare the natural predictors of poisoning and pain.
bank.scenario: Rats made nauseated avoid flavored water, while shocked rats avoid lights and clicking.

bank.definition: Watson and Rayner conditioned fear of a rat by pairing it with a startling metal-clanging noise
bank.hint: Identify which emotional response was learned through stimulus pairing.
bank.scenario: An infant develops fear of a formerly harmless white rat after loud noises accompany it.

bank.definition: A learned fear extends to objects resembling the original feared stimulus
bank.hint: Consider whether a fear remains confined to its training cue.
bank.scenario: A child conditioned to fear a rat also fears a rabbit and a fur collar.

bank.definition: Associating a feared cue with a pleasant or incompatible response to reduce fear
bank.hint: Look for the replacement of fear with another emotional response.
bank.scenario: Mary Cover Jones gives Peter cookies while a rabbit is gradually brought closer.

bank.definition: Prolonged exposure to a harmless feared cue without harm until the fear response diminishes
bank.hint: Think about whether exposure begins at high intensity or progresses gradually.
bank.scenario: A person afraid of harmless spiders remains near one until fear subsides.

bank.definition: Gradual exposure to increasingly feared stimuli while the person remains relaxed
bank.hint: Look for a hierarchy and relaxation together.
bank.scenario: Someone first views photos of dogs and eventually approaches a real dog while practicing relaxation.

bank.definition: Learning in which consequences change the probability of voluntary behaviors
bank.hint: Focus on what happens after a behavior rather than before a reflex.
bank.scenario: A student studies more because studying has repeatedly produced good grades.

bank.definition: Thorndike's principle that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences become more likely
bank.hint: Think about consequences of actions in a puzzle box.
bank.scenario: A cat learns to press the latch that releases it from a puzzle box.

bank.definition: An operant chamber used to study consequences of responses such as lever pressing
bank.hint: Recall laboratory methods used for controlled reinforcement.
bank.scenario: A rat presses a lever in a chamber and receives a food pellet.

bank.definition: Adding a desirable consequence to increase the likelihood of a behavior
bank.hint: The word positive concerns adding something, not whether behavior is moral.
bank.scenario: A teacher gives praise after a student completes homework, increasing homework completion.

bank.definition: Removing an aversive condition to increase the likelihood of a behavior
bank.hint: Check whether removal makes the behavior more frequent.
bank.scenario: Fastening a seat belt silences an annoying buzzer, increasing belt fastening.

bank.definition: Presenting an aversive consequence to reduce the likelihood of a behavior
bank.hint: Decide whether the consequence is added and whether behavior declines.
bank.scenario: Touching a hot stove causes pain, reducing future touching.

bank.definition: Removing a desirable consequence to reduce the likelihood of a behavior
bank.hint: Decide whether something valued is taken away.
bank.scenario: A teenager loses video-game privileges after breaking a rule.

bank.definition: A reinforcer that satisfies a biological need without learning
bank.hint: Think about stimuli relevant to basic bodily needs.
bank.scenario: Food reinforces lever pressing in a hungry rat.

bank.definition: A learned reinforcer valued through its associations with other rewards
bank.hint: Consider why money has reinforcing value.
bank.scenario: A student works for tokens exchangeable for snacks.

bank.definition: Reinforcing successive approximations toward a desired complex response
bank.hint: Imagine rewarding smaller steps toward a final action.
bank.scenario: A trainer rewards a rat first for approaching a lever, then touching it, then pressing it.

bank.definition: Reinforcement delivered after every occurrence of the desired response
bank.scenario: A vending machine reliably dispenses a snack after each valid payment.

bank.definition: Only some occurrences of a behavior are reinforced
bank.hint: Ask whether a reward follows each instance.
bank.scenario: A student receives occasional praise rather than praise after every correct response.

bank.definition: Reinforcement after a predictable number of responses
bank.hint: Does the count of behaviors matter and stay constant?
bank.scenario: A worker receives a bonus after assembling every tenth unit.

bank.definition: Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses
bank.scenario: A gambler wins after a changing and unpredictable number of plays.

bank.definition: The first response after a fixed period of time is reinforced
bank.hint: Ask if time passes in a predictable amount.
bank.scenario: A weekly quiz encourages concentrated studying just before each quiz.

bank.definition: The first response after varying, unpredictable periods is reinforced
bank.hint: Ask if the time intervals change.
bank.scenario: Checking for an email is occasionally rewarded when messages arrive at unpredictable times.

bank.definition: A cue signaling when a particular operant response is likely to be reinforced
bank.hint: Think about how an organism learns when a response will pay off.
bank.scenario: A vending machine's ready light signals that inserting money can produce a snack.

bank.definition: A learned operant behavior declines when it no longer receives reinforcement
bank.hint: Consider what happens when previously rewarding results stop.
bank.scenario: Lever pressing declines after the food dispenser no longer gives pellets.

bank.definition: Using information about physiological processes to learn voluntary regulation of them
bank.hint: Consider feedback from monitoring bodily activity.
bank.scenario: A person watches muscle-tension readings while learning to relax.

bank.definition: Systematically applying learning principles to change targeted behavior
bank.hint: Look for planned use of reinforcement to alter actions.
bank.scenario: A classroom uses points for completing assignments and tracks improvements.

bank.definition: A system where learned tokens are earned for behavior and exchanged for rewards
bank.hint: Check whether symbolic rewards can later buy other reinforcers.
bank.scenario: Patients earn tokens for completing tasks and redeem them for privileges.

bank.definition: Teaching material arranged into small sequential steps with active responses and prompt feedback
bank.hint: Think about pacing and feedback within instruction.
bank.scenario: A learner advances through short instructional frames after responding correctly.

bank.definition: Learning that occurs without immediate reinforcement and may appear later when incentives arise
bank.hint: Can information be acquired without showing it right away?
bank.scenario: An unrewarded rat explores a maze but later runs it efficiently once food is introduced.

bank.definition: A mental representation of the spatial layout of an environment
bank.hint: Think of a remembered route layout.
bank.scenario: A rat takes a new shortcut after learning where maze corridors connect.

bank.definition: Classical conditioning depends on how well one stimulus predicts another, not merely their pairing
bank.hint: Ask whether a cue supplies reliable information about what follows.
bank.scenario: A tone produces stronger learning when it reliably signals the arrival of food.

bank.definition: Learning by watching models and their actions and consequences
bank.hint: Consider imitation and whether the observer experiences the consequence directly.
bank.scenario: A child copies an adult's behavior after seeing the adult rewarded.

bank.definition: Research demonstrating that children can imitate aggressive acts observed in adult models
bank.hint: Recall classic demonstrations about modeling aggression.
bank.scenario: Children reproduce aggressive actions toward an inflatable doll after observing an adult model.

bank.definition: An observer is more likely to imitate a model when the model receives rewards
bank.scenario: A child imitates a peer after seeing the peer praised.

bank.definition: Consciously accessible memory for specific information, also called declarative memory
bank.hint: Think about what can be stated or explained.
bank.scenario: A student recalls a definition and tells it aloud.

bank.definition: Memory of personal events or experiences
bank.hint: Distinguish lived events from general factual knowledge.
bank.scenario: A person remembers what they ate for breakfast yesterday.

bank.definition: Memory for general facts and knowledge
bank.hint: Does the memory concern a personal episode?
bank.scenario: A student knows that Shakespeare wrote Hamlet.

bank.definition: Memory expressed in skills and performance rather than conscious declaration
bank.hint: Think of actions that may be done automatically.
bank.scenario: A person rides a bicycle without explaining each movement.

bank.definition: Remembering to carry out an intention in the future
bank.hint: Does the task involve something not yet done?
bank.scenario: A student remembers to take medicine after dinner.

bank.definition: Remembering information or events from the past
bank.hint: Ask whether the memory concerns an earlier experience.
bank.scenario: A person recalls last week's lecture.

bank.definition: Prior exposure activates associations in memory and facilitates later processing
bank.hint: Consider how encountering something earlier changes later responses.
bank.scenario: Seeing a word earlier makes it easier to complete a related word fragment.

bank.definition: Transforming information into a form that memory can process and retain
bank.hint: Which stage gets incoming information into memory?
bank.scenario: A student turns spoken instructions into a memorable mental image.

bank.definition: Maintaining encoded information over time
bank.scenario: A learned fact is retained until the next week's examination.

bank.definition: Bringing stored information back into awareness or use
bank.hint: Which process brings information out of memory?
bank.scenario: A student recalls an answer during an exam.

bank.definition: Repeating information to keep it active in short-term memory
bank.hint: Compare repeating a number with connecting it to meaning.
bank.scenario: A person silently repeats a phone number until dialing it.

bank.definition: Encoding through meaningful associations with already known information
bank.hint: Does the learner connect material to its meaning?
bank.scenario: A student connects a new term to an example they already understand.

bank.definition: Very brief retention of incoming sensory information
bank.hint: Think about how long a sensory trace remains.
bank.scenario: A visual trace persists for a brief moment after a light disappears.

bank.definition: A fleeting visual sensory memory
bank.hint: Which sense provides the incoming trace?
bank.scenario: A brief afterimage remains when a visual display disappears.

bank.definition: A brief auditory sensory memory
bank.hint: Which sense provides the incoming trace?
bank.scenario: A person can repeat the last few words someone said despite initial inattention.

bank.definition: Temporary memory with limited capacity for information currently being used
bank.hint: Think of holding a small amount of material for a brief period.
bank.scenario: A person holds an unfamiliar code in mind long enough to enter it.

bank.definition: Grouping smaller bits of information into larger meaningful units
bank.hint: Can several items be recoded as a group?
bank.scenario: A learner remembers a long string of digits as three meaningful groups.

bank.definition: Better recall for items appearing at the beginning of a list
bank.hint: Compare earlier items with middle items.
bank.scenario: A student most easily remembers the first terms from a long vocabulary list.

bank.definition: Better recall for items appearing at the end of a list
bank.hint: Compare most recently presented items with middle items.
bank.scenario: A student most easily remembers the final few terms immediately after hearing a list.

bank.definition: The pattern of better recall for early and late items than for middle items
bank.hint: Consider the combined beginning and ending advantage.
bank.scenario: A person recalls the first and last words of a list better than those in the middle.

bank.definition: Competing information disrupts retention of recently held material
bank.hint: Could a second task interfere with a temporary memory?
bank.scenario: A student forgets a code after someone interrupts with a different code.

bank.definition: Relatively durable storage of information over extended periods
bank.hint: Compare storage for seconds with storage for years.
bank.scenario: A person recalls a childhood vacation decades later.

bank.definition: The idea that deeper and more meaningful processing enhances memory
bank.scenario: A student remembers a concept better after explaining its meaning than after focusing only on the font.

bank.definition: A vivid recollection of circumstances surrounding a surprising emotionally significant event
bank.hint: Vividness is not the same as guaranteed accuracy.
bank.scenario: A person clearly recalls where they were when they heard dramatic news.

bank.definition: A temporary inability to retrieve a known word despite a strong feeling of knowing it
bank.hint: Is knowledge lost or momentarily inaccessible?
bank.scenario: A student knows an actor's name but cannot say it until several minutes later.

bank.definition: Retrieval improves when the setting resembles the context of encoding
bank.hint: What environmental cues were present when learning?
bank.scenario: A diver recalls learned words better in the same setting in which they studied.

bank.definition: Retrieval can improve when the internal state matches the state during encoding
bank.hint: Focus on internal rather than external matching cues.
bank.scenario: A person more readily retrieves material when their mood matches their study mood.

bank.definition: Producing information from memory without being shown the target answer
bank.hint: Do the answers appear as choices?
bank.scenario: An exam asks students to write an important definition from memory.

bank.definition: Identifying previously encountered information among presented options
bank.hint: Does the answer appear before the learner?
bank.scenario: A student selects a previously studied name from four options.

bank.definition: Learning previously acquired material again, often faster than the first time
bank.hint: Think about time saved during a second learning attempt.
bank.scenario: A student masters forgotten vocabulary faster on the second study session.

bank.definition: Older memories interfere with learning or retrieving newer information
bank.scenario: An old password makes it difficult to remember a recently changed password.

bank.definition: Newer learning interferes with retention of older information
bank.scenario: Learning a new phone number makes recalling the previous number harder.

bank.definition: Difficulty forming new lasting memories after the onset of amnesia
bank.hint: Which direction in time is impaired?
bank.scenario: After brain injury, a person cannot retain new experiences but recalls childhood.

bank.definition: Loss of memories for events that occurred before the onset of amnesia
bank.hint: Which direction in time is impaired?
bank.scenario: After an accident, a person cannot recall events from the previous month.

bank.definition: Difficulty recalling experiences from very early childhood
bank.hint: Think about memories from the first years of life.
bank.scenario: An adult cannot remember events from their first two years.

bank.definition: In psychoanalytic theory, an unconscious defense process said to block distressing memories
bank.hint: Distinguish a theoretical unconscious defense from ordinary forgetting.
bank.scenario: A psychoanalytic account proposes that a traumatic experience is kept from awareness.

bank.definition: A brain structure important for forming new long-term explicit memories
bank.hint: Recall Henry Molaison's difficulty forming new memories.
bank.scenario: Damage to this structure impairs new declarative memory formation.

bank.definition: A lasting strengthening of synaptic connections following repeated activation
bank.hint: Think about durable changes in neuronal communication.
bank.scenario: Repeated coordinated neural firing makes synaptic signaling more effective.

bank.definition: A brain structure centrally involved in processing emotional significance and emotional memory
bank.hint: Think about fear and emotion in memory.
bank.scenario: An emotionally frightening event engages this structure during memory processing.

bank.definition: A brain structure important for motor learning and some conditioned responses
bank.scenario: Practicing a motor skill depends partly on this structure.

bank.definition: A mental category grouping objects, events, ideas, or qualities with shared properties
bank.hint: Think about how categories make complex information manageable.
bank.scenario: A child groups many different breeds under the category dog.

bank.definition: A particularly representative example of a category
bank.hint: Compare a typical member with an unusual one.
bank.scenario: A robin seems more birdlike than an ostrich to many people.

bank.definition: A specific encountered example used to learn a category
bank.hint: Consider actual examples rather than an abstract summary.
bank.scenario: A teacher shows a child several real dogs to teach the concept dog.

bank.definition: Applying a word or category too broadly to objects outside it
bank.hint: Does a child's category include too much?
bank.scenario: A toddler calls every four-legged animal a dog.

bank.definition: A systematic procedure that guarantees a solution when applied correctly
bank.hint: Compare certainty with a useful shortcut.
bank.scenario: A student follows an exact formula to solve a mathematical problem.

bank.definition: A mental shortcut that simplifies problem solving but does not guarantee a solution
bank.scenario: A person makes an educated guess based on a familiar rule of thumb.

bank.definition: Difficulty seeing a familiar object as useful for a new function
bank.hint: Can the object be used beyond its typical purpose?
bank.scenario: A student fails to consider using a coin as a screwdriver.

bank.definition: A tendency to keep using familiar solutions even when a different approach works better
bank.hint: Look for persistence in an old strategy.
bank.scenario: A learner keeps applying an outdated method to every new puzzle.

bank.definition: Seeking or favoring information that supports existing beliefs
bank.scenario: A person reads only articles supporting an opinion they already hold.

bank.definition: Estimating frequency or probability using how easily examples come to mind
bank.hint: Does a memorable event distort the judgment?
bank.scenario: After watching crash footage, a traveler overestimates the likelihood of a plane crash.

bank.definition: Judging likelihood from resemblance to a typical category rather than base rates
bank.scenario: A person assumes a quiet book lover must be a librarian despite relevant base rates.

bank.definition: Evaluating information in a way influenced by desired conclusions or personal interests
bank.scenario: A fan excuses their favorite team's fouls but condemns identical behavior by rivals.

bank.definition: A structured system of symbols and rules used to communicate meaning
bank.hint: Think about grammar, symbols, and communication.
bank.scenario: People combine words according to shared rules to express new ideas.

bank.definition: A basic speech sound that can distinguish meanings
bank.scenario: Changing the initial sound in bat to p changes the word to pat.

bank.definition: The smallest meaningful unit of language
bank.hint: Ask whether the unit contributes meaning.
bank.scenario: The plural ending s changes cat to cats.

bank.definition: Rules for arranging words into grammatically acceptable sentences
bank.hint: Compare sentence order, not individual sounds.
bank.scenario: The sentence order changes whether a statement is grammatical.

bank.definition: Rules and processes governing meaning in language
bank.hint: Focus on meaning rather than word order.
bank.scenario: A person interprets what the word bank means in a sentence.

bank.definition: The view that language influences how people think about and categorize experience
bank.hint: Consider whether language and cognition shape one another.
bank.scenario: Different language categories affect how readily speakers notice distinctions.

bank.definition: Early infant vocalization involving repeated speechlike sounds
bank.hint: Consider language behavior before meaningful words.
bank.scenario: An infant repeats ba-ba and da-da sounds.

bank.definition: A period when a young child expresses meanings using single words
bank.hint: How many words are used per utterance?
bank.scenario: A toddler says milk to request a drink.

bank.definition: Early multiword speech omitting many function words
bank.scenario: A toddler says mommy go work.

bank.definition: Applying a general grammar rule to an irregular word
bank.hint: Does the child overapply a rule?
bank.scenario: A child says goed instead of went.

bank.definition: Chomsky's proposed innate capacity that supports language acquisition
bank.hint: Consider nature's role in language development.
bank.scenario: A theory proposes that children possess inborn language-learning capacities.

bank.definition: The ability to use two languages
bank.hint: Focus on command of more than one linguistic system.
bank.scenario: A child communicates at home in one language and at school in another.

bank.definition: Spearman's proposed common factor contributing to performance across cognitive tasks
bank.hint: Look for the shared ingredient across tests.
bank.scenario: A theory posits a common mental ability behind diverse intellectual tasks.

bank.definition: Gardner's proposal of several relatively distinct kinds of intelligence
bank.hint: Think about more than one domain of ability.
bank.scenario: A teacher considers musical, interpersonal, and spatial abilities alongside linguistic skills.

bank.definition: Sternberg's model distinguishing analytical, creative, and practical intelligence
bank.hint: Think about three complementary kinds of intelligent performance.
bank.scenario: A student is skilled at test problems, inventing ideas, and handling real-life situations.

bank.definition: The capacity to perceive, understand, and manage emotions
bank.scenario: A student notices others' distress and regulates their own emotional reaction.

bank.definition: The ability to produce novel and useful ideas or solutions
bank.scenario: A learner develops an unusual but workable solution to a problem.

bank.definition: A standardized score expressing intellectual test performance relative to age peers
bank.hint: Think about interpretation of a standardized ability score.
bank.scenario: A psychologist reports an age-normed score from an intelligence test.

bank.definition: An individually administered intelligence test developed from Binet's approach
bank.hint: Think of historically foundational individual intelligence testing.
bank.scenario: An examiner gives one person a battery derived from Binet's intelligence measures.

bank.definition: A family of intelligence tests providing scores across distinct cognitive domains
bank.hint: Think about commonly used individual intelligence assessment batteries.
bank.scenario: A clinician uses an adult intelligence battery with multiple cognitive indexes.

bank.definition: Consistency of a psychological measurement across occasions or items
bank.hint: A test can be consistent without measuring the right trait.
bank.scenario: Students receive similar scores when taking comparable versions of an assessment.

bank.definition: The extent to which a test measures or supports its intended interpretation
bank.hint: Ask whether a measure assesses what it claims.
bank.scenario: A reasoning test actually predicts or measures the reasoning construct it targets.

bank.definition: Uniform procedures and normative comparisons in testing
bank.hint: Think about fair administration and scoring conditions.
bank.scenario: An assessment uses the same instructions and comparison norms for everyone.

bank.definition: The proportion of variation in a trait within a population attributable statistically to genetic differences
bank.hint: This statistic is about variation in a population, not one person's destiny.
bank.scenario: Researchers estimate how much individual variation in test scores is associated with genes in a particular population.

bank.definition: Effects of experience and conditions such as education and nutrition on intellectual performance
bank.hint: Consider what changes outside the genome.
bank.scenario: A child's educational opportunities and nutrition affect cognitive development.

bank.definition: Research designs used to estimate genetic and environmental contributions to individual differences
bank.hint: Compare people differing in genetic relatedness and upbringing.
bank.scenario: Researchers compare identical twins raised apart when examining cognitive abilities.

bank.definition: Computer systems performing tasks associated with human cognitive abilities
bank.hint: Think of machine performance on reasoning or language tasks.
bank.scenario: A software system generates responses and solves problems using learned patterns.

bank.definition: An inferred internal state that activates behavior and directs it toward a goal
bank.hint: Think of an underlying why behind behavior.
bank.scenario: A student persists in studying because they want academic success.

bank.definition: A state of deprivation that can motivate behavior
bank.hint: What condition exists before a drive emerges?
bank.scenario: A person has gone many hours without water.

bank.definition: An aroused condition associated with a need that prompts action
bank.hint: Distinguish deprivation from the resulting activation.
bank.scenario: A thirsty person's discomfort motivates finding water.

bank.definition: An external object, person, or situation perceived as rewarding or desirable
bank.hint: Does the motivation arise from something outside the organism?
bank.scenario: A prize encourages students to enter a competition.

bank.definition: A requirement linked to biological survival or bodily regulation
bank.hint: Think of oxygen, food, water, and temperature.
bank.scenario: A person needs water after prolonged exertion.

bank.definition: A desire such as achievement, belonging, or social approval
bank.hint: Consider needs shaped by personal experiences and culture.
bank.scenario: A person works to feel accepted by a social group.

bank.definition: An inherited predisposition toward species-typical patterns of behavior
bank.hint: Think of behavior present without individual training.
bank.scenario: A spider spins a web without being taught.

bank.definition: A relatively stereotyped innate sequence triggered by particular stimuli
bank.scenario: A male betta fish displays characteristic threatening postures to another male.

bank.definition: The theory that organisms learn behaviors that lower biological or acquired drive tension
bank.hint: Think about relief from bodily tension.
bank.scenario: A thirsty person drinks to reduce an uncomfortable drive.

bank.definition: The tendency to maintain a stable internal physiological state
bank.hint: Think of a thermostat correcting departures from a set point.
bank.scenario: The body regulates temperature near an operating range.

bank.definition: The idea that people seek a suitable rather than minimal level of stimulation
bank.scenario: A person seeks a challenging activity after hours of monotony.

bank.definition: A humanistic model arranging needs from basic physiological concerns toward growth and self-actualization
bank.hint: Think about needs grouped by their priority.
bank.scenario: A student struggling for food finds it hard to prioritize personal fulfillment.

bank.definition: Fulfilling one's potential and developing one's capacities
bank.hint: Think about growth beyond meeting basic needs.
bank.scenario: An artist pursues a meaningful creative calling for personal growth.

bank.definition: Engaging in an activity for inherent interest or enjoyment
bank.hint: Would the person do it without external rewards?
bank.scenario: A student reads astronomy books because they love the subject.

bank.definition: Engaging in an activity to obtain an external reward or avoid a consequence
bank.hint: Is the purpose separate from the activity?
bank.scenario: A student studies primarily for prize money.

bank.definition: A brain region important in regulating hunger and bodily homeostasis
bank.hint: Think of a central regulatory brain area.
bank.scenario: Changes in brain mechanisms alter appetite and energy regulation.

bank.definition: A hormone associated with fat stores that informs the brain about energy availability
bank.hint: Consider signals sent by body fat.
bank.scenario: Fat tissue releases a signal relevant to long-term energy regulation.

bank.definition: A hormone from the gastrointestinal system involved in stimulating hunger
bank.hint: Consider signals that rise around meal timing.
bank.scenario: A stomach-related hormone contributes to feelings of hunger before eating.

bank.definition: The proposal that the body regulates weight around a biologically influenced level
bank.hint: Think of weight regulation and homeostasis.
bank.scenario: After weight loss, regulatory responses tend to oppose further weight change.

bank.definition: Environmental signals that influence eating beyond internal hunger
bank.hint: Consider appearance, smell, time, and availability of food.
bank.scenario: A person eats dessert after a full meal because it smells appealing.

bank.definition: An eating disorder marked by significantly low weight, restrictive eating, and intense fear of weight gain or related body-image disturbance
bank.hint: Distinguish restriction and low weight from episodes of bingeing.
bank.scenario: A person persistently restricts intake despite being markedly underweight.

bank.definition: An eating disorder involving recurrent binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors
bank.hint: Look for both binge episodes and attempts to compensate.
bank.scenario: After a binge, a person repeatedly induces vomiting to avoid weight gain.

bank.definition: Recurrent binge episodes with loss of control without regular compensatory behavior
bank.hint: Check whether compensation routinely follows a binge.
bank.scenario: A person repeatedly eats unusually large amounts with loss of control but does not purge.

bank.definition: A distorted or excessively negative evaluation of one's body shape or weight
bank.hint: Think of perception and self-evaluation, not just body mass.
bank.scenario: An individual perceives their body as unacceptable despite reassurance.

bank.definition: Motivation to master tasks and meet standards of excellence
bank.hint: Focus on the drive to accomplish challenging goals.
bank.scenario: A student sets difficult but realistic learning goals for personal accomplishment.

bank.definition: A tendency to strive toward successful performance and high standards
bank.hint: Consider why a person persists at demanding tasks.
bank.scenario: An athlete practices consistently to improve performance.

bank.definition: External rewards can undermine intrinsic interest in an already enjoyable activity
bank.hint: Could a reward change the reason one does a task?
bank.scenario: A child loses interest in drawing for fun after regularly being paid to draw.

bank.definition: A psychological and physiological state involving feelings, bodily arousal, and expression
bank.scenario: A frightening event produces fear, a racing heart, and facial expression.

bank.definition: The proposal that facial-muscle activity can influence emotional experience
bank.hint: Ask whether expression can alter feeling.
bank.scenario: Holding a smile may influence how a person experiences a pleasant event.

bank.definition: Socially learned norms about when and how emotions should be expressed
bank.scenario: A person suppresses visible anger during a formal meeting.

bank.definition: The study of strengths, well-being, positive experiences, and flourishing
bank.hint: Think about more than illness reduction.
bank.scenario: Researchers study gratitude, life satisfaction, and resilience.

bank.definition: People's evaluations and emotional experiences of their lives, including life satisfaction
bank.hint: Consider both feelings and judgments about life.
bank.scenario: A researcher asks about happiness and satisfaction with life.

bank.definition: Positive subjective experience associated with well-being and life satisfaction
bank.hint: Think about emotional and evaluative components.
bank.scenario: A person reports frequent positive emotions and satisfaction with life.

bank.definition: The theory that emotion is experienced through perception of physiological reactions to events
bank.hint: Which comes first in the proposed sequence?
bank.scenario: A person notices their trembling body and then experiences fear.

bank.definition: The theory that emotional experience and physiological arousal occur simultaneously
bank.hint: Think about parallel emotional and bodily reactions.
bank.scenario: A frightening sight triggers fear and bodily arousal at the same time.

bank.definition: The theory that emotion depends on physiological arousal and cognitive labeling of that arousal
bank.scenario: Someone interprets a racing heart in context to decide whether they feel fear or excitement.

bank.definition: The view that evaluation of an event contributes centrally to the emotional reaction
bank.hint: Think about how interpreting a situation can shape emotion.
bank.scenario: Two people respond differently to the same event because they appraise it differently.

bank.definition: The fertilized egg formed by union of sperm and ovum
bank.hint: Think about the earliest one-cell stage.
bank.scenario: A sperm fertilizes an egg, producing a single new cell.

bank.definition: Prenatal period from conception through implantation
bank.hint: Which stage includes travel to the uterus and implantation?
bank.scenario: A fertilized egg divides while moving toward and implanting in the uterus.

bank.definition: Prenatal period from implantation until about eight weeks, when major organ systems begin forming
bank.hint: Consider organ system formation during early pregnancy.
bank.scenario: Major organs begin forming in an implanted developing organism.

bank.definition: Prenatal stage from the beginning of the third month until birth
bank.hint: Which stage extends through later pregnancy?
bank.scenario: A developing organism grows from the third month of pregnancy to birth.

bank.definition: Growth and development proceeding from head toward tail
bank.scenario: The head develops ahead of lower body regions.

bank.definition: Growth and development proceeding from central axis outward to extremities
bank.hint: Think near to far from the central body axis.
bank.scenario: Upper arms develop before forearms and hands.

bank.definition: An organ through which nutrients and wastes are exchanged between the mother and developing organism
bank.scenario: A prenatal structure supports exchange of oxygen and nutrients.

bank.definition: A fluid-filled protective sac surrounding the developing embryo or fetus
bank.hint: What cushions movement and helps regulate temperature?
bank.scenario: A fetus moves safely within a protective fluid environment.

bank.definition: An automatic unlearned response to a stimulus
bank.hint: Does the infant need deliberate practice to show the response?
bank.scenario: A newborn automatically sucks when its mouth is stimulated.

bank.definition: A newborn response of turning toward touch near the cheek or mouth
bank.scenario: A newborn turns toward a touched cheek to seek a nipple.

bank.definition: An infant startle response involving sudden extension and movement of the limbs
bank.hint: Consider reactions to unexpected loss of support.
bank.scenario: A baby throws out its arms when abruptly startled.

bank.definition: An infant response of closing fingers around an object touching the palm
bank.scenario: A baby tightly grips a finger placed in its palm.

bank.definition: Progressive acquisition of abilities to control movement and posture
bank.hint: Think sitting, crawling, standing, and walking.
bank.scenario: An infant progresses from sitting to standing and then walking.

bank.definition: An apparatus used to investigate infants' perception of depth
bank.hint: Think about avoiding an apparent drop-off.
bank.scenario: An infant hesitates to crawl over what appears to be a steep drop.

bank.definition: A mental framework used to organize and interpret information
bank.hint: Think of mental categories that change with experience.
bank.scenario: A child has a mental framework for what a dog is.

bank.definition: Interpreting new experiences using existing schemas
bank.hint: Does the existing mental framework stay largely intact?
bank.scenario: A toddler calls a new breed of dog a dog using an existing concept.

bank.definition: Modifying a schema to fit information that does not match it
bank.hint: Does the child's internal category need revision?
bank.scenario: A child learns that a horse is not a dog and revises their categories.

bank.definition: Piaget's earliest stage when infants learn through sensory and motor actions
bank.scenario: A baby repeatedly shakes a toy to explore its sound.

bank.definition: Understanding that objects continue to exist when they cannot be seen
bank.hint: Does absence from view mean absence from existence?
bank.scenario: An infant searches for a toy hidden under a cloth.

bank.definition: Piaget's stage characterized by symbolic thinking but limited logical operations
bank.hint: Think preschool reasoning and symbolic play.
bank.scenario: A preschooler uses a banana as a pretend telephone.

bank.definition: Difficulty taking another person's point of view in early cognitive development
bank.scenario: A child assumes everyone sees the same view they see.

bank.definition: Understanding that quantity remains constant despite changes in shape or appearance
bank.hint: Has anything been added or removed?
bank.scenario: A child recognizes that water volume is unchanged when poured into a taller glass.

bank.definition: Piaget's stage of logical reasoning about tangible and concrete situations
bank.hint: Think about conservation and reasoning with real objects.
bank.scenario: A school-age child understands that reshaped clay retains its amount.

bank.definition: Piaget's stage associated with abstract and hypothetical reasoning
bank.hint: Can the learner reason about possibilities rather than only objects?
bank.scenario: An adolescent systematically tests hypothetical explanations.

bank.definition: Vygotsky's range of tasks possible with assistance but not yet alone
bank.hint: Compare independent performance with supported performance.
bank.scenario: A learner completes a difficult puzzle only with a skilled adult's guidance.

bank.definition: Temporary instructional support adjusted as the learner becomes more capable
bank.hint: Think about guidance that can be gradually withdrawn.
bank.scenario: A teacher gives hints early and removes them as the student masters the task.

bank.definition: Moral reasoning organized mainly around punishment and personal reward
bank.hint: Think of immediate consequences for the individual.
bank.scenario: A child calls an act wrong primarily because it leads to punishment.

bank.definition: Moral reasoning that emphasizes social approval, rules, and maintaining order
bank.scenario: A teenager argues that obeying rules maintains societal order.

bank.definition: Moral reasoning emphasizing broad principles and rights beyond particular rules
bank.hint: Think of ethical principles that can challenge laws.
bank.scenario: A person criticizes an unjust law using universal ethical principles.

bank.definition: Erikson's infancy crisis centering on dependable care and security
bank.hint: Which developmental period depends heavily on caregiver reliability?
bank.scenario: Consistent caregiving helps an infant feel the world is safe.

bank.definition: Erikson's early-childhood crisis concerning independent action and self-control
bank.hint: Think of toddlers attempting tasks alone.
bank.scenario: A toddler insists on dressing without assistance.

bank.definition: Erikson's preschool-age crisis involving initiative in activities and goals
bank.hint: Think of creating plans and starting activities.
bank.scenario: A preschool child organizes a make-believe game.

bank.definition: Erikson's school-age crisis involving competence in work and skills
bank.hint: Think of mastery in school and tasks.
bank.scenario: A child feels capable after mastering multiplication.

bank.definition: Erikson's adolescent crisis concerning forming a coherent personal identity
bank.hint: Think about exploration of values and roles.
bank.scenario: An adolescent explores interests and future roles to develop a stable identity.

bank.definition: A caregiver-child bond marked by confidence in availability and comfort when reunited
bank.hint: Consider a safe base for exploration.
bank.scenario: An infant explores when a caregiver is nearby and is soothed after reunion.

bank.definition: Parenting combining warmth and responsiveness with firm, reasonable expectations
bank.hint: Consider support together with consistent boundaries.
bank.scenario: Parents explain rules while listening to their child's concerns.

bank.definition: Parenting high in control and demands but low in warmth and dialogue
bank.hint: Look for strict obedience with little discussion.
bank.scenario: A parent demands unquestioned obedience and discourages discussion.

bank.definition: Parenting high in warmth but low in rules and behavioral demands
bank.hint: Look for affection without consistent limits.
bank.scenario: A caring parent rarely enforces boundaries.

bank.definition: Parenting low in both responsiveness and behavioral demands
bank.scenario: A parent offers little emotional involvement or supervision.

bank.definition: Biological changes leading to sexual maturity during adolescence
bank.hint: Think of the physical transition during adolescence.
bank.scenario: An adolescent develops secondary sex characteristics.

bank.definition: Heightened focus on one's own experiences and on how others perceive oneself
bank.hint: Think about the adolescent's sense of being watched or unique.
bank.scenario: A teenager assumes everyone notices a tiny blemish on their face.

bank.definition: The belief that others are intensely observing and evaluating one's appearance or actions
bank.hint: Does the teen feel constantly watched?
bank.scenario: A teenager thinks the whole class is staring at a new haircut.

bank.definition: The belief that one's own experiences are uniquely special or that one is unusually invulnerable
bank.hint: Consider the adolescent's sense of being exceptional.
bank.scenario: A teenager believes risks apply to everyone except them.

bank.definition: The process of examining values, goals, relationships, and future roles
bank.hint: Think of choices shaping personal identity.
bank.scenario: A student explores different career paths and moral values.

bank.definition: A transitional period after adolescence involving exploration of adult roles and responsibilities
bank.hint: Consider gradual steps toward stable adult roles.
bank.scenario: A young adult explores education, work, relationships, and independence.

bank.definition: Experimentation with commitments in work, love, and worldview during the transition to adulthood
bank.hint: Think of several possibilities before stable commitments.
bank.scenario: A young adult tries different occupations and relationships.

bank.definition: Erikson's middle-adulthood conflict concerning contributing to future generations versus feeling unproductive
bank.hint: Think about investing in others beyond oneself.
bank.scenario: A middle-aged adult mentors younger colleagues and raises children.

bank.definition: Erikson's late-adulthood conflict about accepting one's life versus regretting it
bank.hint: Think about reflection on one's whole life.
bank.scenario: An older adult feels peace when reviewing a meaningful life.

bank.definition: Reasoning and solving novel problems without relying heavily on learned knowledge
bank.scenario: An adult solves an unfamiliar abstract pattern puzzle.

bank.definition: Accumulated learned knowledge and skills developed through experience
bank.hint: Think about vocabulary and general knowledge.
bank.scenario: An older adult relies on decades of vocabulary and expertise.

bank.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative condition involving cognitive decline, not a normal consequence of aging
bank.hint: Separate disease from ordinary age-related change.
bank.scenario: An older adult develops worsening impairment in memory and daily functioning.

bank.definition: The family-life transition when children leave the parental home
bank.hint: Consider adjustment to changed household roles.
bank.scenario: Parents adapt after their youngest child moves out.

bank.definition: Increased responsiveness to a stimulus following repeated or intense exposure
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of sensitization and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: After hearing a frightening crash, a student startles at even soft noises.

bank.definition: Learning results from experience, whereas maturation results from biological development
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of learning versus maturation and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A baby's ability to walk appears partly because the nervous system develops, not simply because of training.

bank.definition: Researcher whose dog experiments established the principles of classical conditioning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of pavlov and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A scientist pairs a tone with meat powder until the tone alone elicits salivation.

bank.definition: The conditioned stimulus occurs before the unconditioned stimulus and predicts it
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of forward conditioning and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A bell rings immediately before food appears on each trial.

bank.definition: An emotional reaction acquired through classical conditioning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of conditioned emotional response and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Someone feels anxious when entering the room where they previously had a frightening experience.

bank.definition: Conditioned responding tends to weaken as the test stimulus becomes less similar to the original CS
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of generalization gradient and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A dog salivates most to the trained tone and less to increasingly different pitches.

bank.term: Conditioned taste aversion after one trial

bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of conditioned taste aversion after one trial and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: After one episode of food poisoning a person avoids that meal for years.

bank.definition: Evolutionary predispositions make some stimulus-response associations easier to learn
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of biological constraints on conditioning and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: An animal readily associates an unfamiliar flavor with illness but not a flashing light.

bank.definition: Psychologist associated with reducing children's fears through counterconditioning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of mary cover jones and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A child gradually tolerates a rabbit when it is paired with pleasant food.

bank.definition: Fear treatment that proceeds through increasingly challenging encounters with a feared stimulus
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of graduated exposure and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Someone first imagines an elevator, then approaches one, then rides it.

bank.definition: In systematic desensitization, relaxation is paired with gradual exposure to feared situations
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of relaxation with exposure and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A person practices deep relaxation while progressing through a fear hierarchy.

bank.definition: Psychologist who proposed that satisfying consequences strengthen behavior through the law of effect
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of edward thorndike and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A cat escapes a puzzle box faster after previous successful trials.

bank.definition: Psychologist who analyzed operant behavior and its consequences
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of b. f. skinner and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A researcher records lever pressing in a chamber that delivers food pellets.

bank.definition: Reinforcement increases future behavior whereas punishment decreases future behavior
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of reinforcement versus punishment and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student distinguishes rewards that strengthen attendance from consequences that reduce tardiness.

bank.definition: Positive means adding a stimulus, whereas negative means removing one
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of positive versus negative consequences and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A car's beeping stops once the driver fastens the seat belt.

bank.definition: A response terminates an ongoing unpleasant stimulus
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of escape learning and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A rat presses a lever to switch off an electric shock.

bank.definition: A response prevents a predicted unpleasant stimulus from occurring
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of avoidance learning and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student leaves early to avoid being late and reprimanded.

bank.definition: Behaviors reinforced intermittently often persist longer without reward than continuously reinforced behaviors
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of partial-reinforcement extinction effect and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A slot machine player continues despite repeated losses.

bank.definition: Fixed schedules follow predictable counts or times whereas variable schedules fluctuate
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of fixed versus variable schedules and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A sales bonus after exactly five sales is contrasted with unpredictable payouts.

bank.definition: Ratio schedules depend on responses whereas interval schedules depend on elapsed time
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of ratio versus interval schedules and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A commission paid per item is compared with checking for a message after time has elapsed.

bank.definition: Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase a behavior is not punishment
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of negative reinforcement versus punishment and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Taking pain medication makes a headache disappear, reinforcing medication-taking.

bank.definition: Teaching a complex sequence by linking individually learned responses
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of chaining and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A rat learns to climb, cross a bridge and press a lever in a specific sequence.

bank.definition: Small steps toward a target behavior are reinforced in shaping
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of successive approximations and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A trainer first rewards turning toward a ball, then approaching it, then retrieving it.

bank.definition: A symbolic reward acquires value because it can be exchanged for desired goods
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of token as conditioned reinforcer and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Students earn points exchangeable for extra activities.

bank.definition: An intervention specifies target behaviors and their consequences
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of behavior modification contingency and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A teacher rewards completed homework rather than merely telling students to work harder.

bank.definition: Psychologist whose maze studies supported latent learning and cognitive maps
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of edward tolman and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A rat explores a maze without rewards but later finds food quickly.

bank.definition: Psychologist who emphasized the predictiveness of the conditioned stimulus in classical conditioning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of robert rescorla and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A tone produces stronger learning when it reliably signals that food is coming.

bank.definition: Psychologist known for social learning and the Bobo doll research
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of albert bandura and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Children imitate aggression shown by an adult model.

bank.definition: Attention, retention, reproduction and motivation influence successful modeling
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of four observational learning processes and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student watches a procedure, remembers it, can perform it and has a reason to try.

bank.definition: Observing a model punished decreases an observer's likelihood of imitating that behavior
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of vicarious punishment and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A child avoids a prank after seeing another student disciplined for doing it.

bank.definition: Sudden recognition of a solution rather than gradual trial and error
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of insight learning and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A chimp suddenly stacks boxes to reach suspended food.

bank.definition: Another name for explicit memory of facts and personal events
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of declarative memory and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A person consciously explains the capital of a country.

bank.definition: Implicit memory for learned skills and how to carry out actions
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of procedural memory and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A person rides a bicycle automatically after years without practice.

bank.definition: The episodic record of personally experienced events
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of autobiographical memory and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student recalls a particular birthday celebration.

bank.definition: A person whose severe new-memory difficulties after brain surgery advanced memory research
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of henry molaison h.m. and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Following surgery, a patient learns a motor skill but cannot remember practicing it.

bank.definition: A person may demonstrate a learned skill despite lacking conscious recollection of learning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of implicit versus explicit dissociation and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A patient improves at mirror tracing but reports never having done it.

bank.definition: Representing material in memory based on its sound
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of acoustic encoding and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: Someone remembers a number by repeating its spoken rhythm.

bank.definition: Representing material based on its appearance
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of visual encoding and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student imagines the spelling of a word.

bank.definition: Representing information by its meaning
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of semantic encoding and distinguish it from nearby concepts.
bank.scenario: A student links the idea of homeostasis to an everyday thermostat.

bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of authoritative versus authoritarian and distinguish it from nearby concepts.

bank.definition: Preschool-age challenge involving goal-directed activities and possible guilt about initiative
bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of erikson initiative versus guilt and distinguish it from nearby concepts.

bank.scenario: A teenager gains several centimeters within a year.

bank.hint: Identify the defining feature of adolescent risk perception and distinguish it from nearby concepts.

bank.q: What is the id?
bank.a: The structure, present at birth, that represents biological drives and is fully unconscious
d: The structure that uses reason to satisfy the id's demands without drawing social disapproval
The moral guardian that develops as the child takes in the standards of parents and others
The part of the mind holding ideas that can be made conscious by focusing on them
bank.why: The id is present at birth, represents biological drives (sex, aggression) and is entirely unconscious.
dh: The structure, present at birth, that represents biological drives and is partly conscious and partly unconscious
The structure, developing in the first year, that represents biological drives and is fully unconscious
The structure, present at birth, that represents moral standards and is fully unconscious
bank.xq: Freud believed that a newborn's behavior is driven entirely by one psychic structure, which demands instant gratification of its needs and has no contact with reason or morality. Which of the following correctly describes this structure, including when it appears, what it represents and how much of it is conscious?

dw.The structure that uses reason to satisf: That describes the ego, which uses reason to satisfy the id.
dw.The moral guardian that develops as the: That describes the superego, the moral guardian.
dw.The part of the mind holding ideas that: That describes the preconscious: ideas you can recall by focusing.

bank.q: What is the ego?
bank.a: The structure that uses reason to satisfy the id's demands without drawing social disapproval
d: The structure, present at birth, that represents biological drives and is fully unconscious
The moral guardian that develops as the child takes in the standards of parents and others
The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges kept out of awareness
bank.why: The ego stands for reason and good sense; it curbs the id and seeks gratification while avoiding social disapproval.
dh: The structure that uses reason to block the id's demands so it never draws social disapproval
The structure that uses moral standards to satisfy the id's demands without drawing social disapproval
The structure that uses reason to satisfy the superego's demands without drawing social disapproval
bank.xq: According to Freud, as a child grows, one psychic structure develops to take the id's raw demands and find realistic ways to meet them, so that the person can get what they want without getting into trouble with others. Which of the following best describes this structure?

dw.The structure, present at birth, that re: That is the id, present at birth and driven by biology.
dw.The moral guardian that develops as the: That is the superego, the moral guardian.
dw.The part of the mind holding primitive i: That is the unconscious mind, where urges are kept out of awareness.

bank.q: What is the superego?
bank.a: The moral guardian that develops as the child takes in the standards of parents and others
d: The structure, present at birth, that represents biological drives and is fully unconscious
The structure that uses reason to satisfy the id's demands without drawing social disapproval
A store of primitive images, or archetypes, that reflects the history of the species
bank.why: The superego develops through identification with parents and moral figures and judges right and wrong.
dh: The moral guardian, present at birth, that holds the standards of parents and others
The rational guardian that develops as the child takes in the standards of parents and others
The moral guardian that develops as the child takes in the demands of the id
bank.xq: A child who once grabbed toys freely begins to feel that taking things is wrong, even when no adult is watching, because she has made her parents' rules her own. Which statement best describes the psychic structure Freud said is forming in her?

dw.The structure, present at birth, that re: That is the id: biological drives, present at birth.
dw.The structure that uses reason to satisf: That is the ego, which works by reason.
dw.A store of primitive images, or archetyp: That is Jung's collective unconscious, not a Freudian structure.

bank.q: In Freud's view, what is the preconscious?
bank.a: The part of the mind holding ideas that can be made conscious by focusing on them
d: The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges kept out of awareness
The part of the mind that holds what you are aware of right now
The structure, present at birth, that represents biological drives and is fully unconscious
bank.why: Example: what you ate three days ago is out of awareness, but you can recall it by focusing on it.
dh: The part of the mind holding ideas that can never be made conscious, even by focusing on them
The part of the mind holding the ideas you are focusing on right now
The part of the mind holding repressed urges that can be made conscious by focusing on them
bank.xq: A student cannot think of her grade-school best friend's name while focused on an exam, but when she later stops and concentrates on her childhood, the name comes back to her. In Freud's model of the mind, which description fits the level where that memory had been waiting?

dw.The part of the mind holding primitive i: That is the unconscious: it stays out of awareness even when you focus.
dw.The part of the mind that holds what you: That is the conscious mind: what you are aware of right now.
dw.The structure, present at birth, that re: That is the id, a structure of personality, not a level of awareness.

bank.q: In Freud's view, what is the unconscious mind?
bank.a: The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges kept out of awareness
d: The part of the mind holding ideas that can be made conscious by focusing on them
The part of the mind that holds what you are aware of right now
The moral guardian that develops as the child takes in the standards of parents and others
bank.why: The unconscious holds primitive instincts such as sex and aggression and urges kept down by repression.
dh: The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges that can be recalled by focusing on them
The part of the mind holding learned rules and moral standards kept out of awareness
The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges that you are aware of right now
bank.xq: Freud compared the mind to an iceberg, with most of it hidden below the surface. Which of the following best describes what Freud placed in the deepest, hidden part of the mind?

dw.The part of the mind holding ideas that: That is the preconscious: you can recall it by focusing.
dw.The part of the mind that holds what you: That is the conscious mind: what you notice right now.
dw.The moral guardian that develops as the: That is the superego, a structure of personality, not a level of awareness.

bank.q: Which structure of personality follows the pleasure principle?
bank.a: Id
d: Ego
Superego
Preconscious
bank.why: The id demands instant gratification without regard for law, custom or other people.
bank.xq: Freud described each of the three structures of personality as operating on a different principle. One structure seeks immediate gratification of its impulses and does not care about reality, rules or consequences. Which structure follows this pleasure principle?

dw.Ego: The ego follows the reality principle.
dw.Superego: The superego follows the moral principle.
dw.Preconscious: The preconscious is a level of awareness, not a structure with a principle.

bank.q: Which structure of personality is guided by the reality principle?
bank.a: Ego
d: Id
Superego
Libido
bank.why: The ego takes into account what is practical along with what the id urges.
bank.xq: In Freud's theory, one structure takes into account what is practical and possible, weighing what can actually be done and delaying gratification until it is safe. Which structure of personality is guided by this reality principle?

dw.Id: The id follows the pleasure principle.
dw.Superego: The superego follows the moral principle.
dw.Libido: Libido is psychic energy, not a structure.

bank.q: Which structure functions according to the moral principle?
bank.a: Superego
d: Ego
Id
Eros
bank.why: The superego holds up an ideal self and floods the ego with guilt and shame when standards are not met.
bank.xq: Freud said one structure of personality judges whether the person's thoughts and actions are right or wrong, and punishes wrongdoing with feelings of guilt. Which structure functions according to this moral principle?

dw.Ego: The ego follows the reality principle.
dw.Id: The id follows the pleasure principle.
dw.Eros: Eros is the life instinct, not a structure.

bank.q: You are starving and pass a store. An urge says to grab a candy bar and eat it now, without paying. Which structure is speaking?
bank.a: Id
d: Ego
Superego
Preconscious mind
bank.why: Wanting it now, regardless of law or other people, is the pleasure principle of the id.
bank.xq: You skipped lunch and are starving as you walk past a convenience store. Before you can even think it through, an urge inside you says to grab a candy bar off the shelf and eat it right now, without paying and without caring what happens next. According to Freud, which structure of personality is speaking?

dw.Ego: The ego would weigh the consequences before grabbing it.
dw.Superego: The superego would say stealing is wrong.
dw.Preconscious mind: The preconscious is a level of awareness, not a voice demanding gratification.

bank.q: You want the candy bar, but you take it to the counter and pay, getting what you want without breaking the law. Which structure decided this?
bank.a: Ego
d: Id
Superego
Libido
bank.why: The ego finds a realistic way to satisfy the id while avoiding disapproval.
bank.xq: Still hungry, you want the candy bar badly, but you realize that stealing it could get you arrested. So you take it to the counter, pay for it, and eat it outside, getting what you want in a way that does not break the law. Which structure of personality made this decision?

dw.Id: The id wanted it now, whatever the rules.
dw.Superego: The superego judges right and wrong; this was a realistic compromise.
dw.Libido: Libido is energy, not a structure that decides.

bank.q: After telling a small lie, a student feels guilty for the rest of the day. Which structure produces the guilt?
bank.a: Superego
d: Ego
Id
Unconscious
bank.why: The superego judges right and wrong and creates guilt when its standards are not met.
bank.xq: A student tells a small lie to her teacher to get an extension. Nobody finds out, and nothing bad happens to her, yet she feels guilty and uneasy for the rest of the day. In Freud's theory, which structure of personality is producing this guilt?

dw.Ego: The ego finds realistic solutions; guilt comes from the superego.
dw.Id: The id seeks pleasure and feels no guilt.
dw.Unconscious: The unconscious is a level of awareness; guilt is produced by a structure, the superego.

bank.q: What is repression?
bank.a: The automatic ejection of anxiety-evoking ideas from awareness
d: Talking freely about anything that comes to mind to explore the unconscious
Channeling sexual energy into nonsexual, socially acceptable activities
Identifying with the parent of the same gender to resolve a conflict
bank.why: Repression is a defense mechanism used by the ego. Many investigators now see it as more myth than fact.
dh: The deliberate pushing of anxiety-evoking ideas out of awareness
The automatic ejection of anxiety-evoking ideas onto other people
The automatic channeling of anxiety-evoking ideas into acceptable activities
bank.xq: A man who was bitten by a dog as a small child has no memory of the event at all, even though it still makes him uneasy around dogs. Freud would say this anxiety-provoking memory was removed from awareness. Which of the following correctly describes this defense mechanism?

dw.Talking freely about anything that comes: That is free association, used in psychoanalysis.
dw.Channeling sexual energy into nonsexual,: That is sublimation: redirecting urges into acceptable activity.
dw.Identifying with the parent of the same: That is identification, how the Oedipus or Electra conflict is resolved.

bank.q: As a way of studying personality, what is psychoanalysis?
bank.a: Exploring the unconscious by having people talk freely about whatever comes to mind
d: The automatic ejection of anxiety-evoking ideas from conscious awareness into the unconscious
A questionnaire whose items have specific, limited answers scored as correct
Observing behavior in a natural setting without interfering with what people do
bank.why: In psychoanalysis people talk about anything that pops into mind while comfortable and relaxed.
dh: Exploring the preconscious by having people talk freely about whatever comes to mind
Exploring the unconscious by having people answer true–false items about themselves
Exploring the conscious mind by having people report only what they are thinking right now
bank.xq: Freud's patients lay on a couch and were encouraged to say anything that came to mind, however silly or embarrassing, while Freud listened for clues to what lay hidden beneath. As a method of studying personality, which statement best describes psychoanalysis?

dw.The automatic ejection of anxiety-evokin: That is repression, a defense mechanism.
dw.A questionnaire whose items have specifi: That describes an objective personality test.

bank.q: What is eros?
bank.a: The major instinct that aims to preserve and perpetuate life
d: The psychic energy, or sex drive, that fuels this instinct
A part of the body that is sensitive to sexual stimulation
Excessive or insufficient gratification in a stage of development
bank.why: Eros is the life instinct; libido is the energy that fuels it.
dh: The major instinct that aims to return life to an inanimate state
The psychic energy, or sex drive, that aims to preserve and perpetuate life
The minor instinct that aims to preserve and perpetuate pleasure
bank.xq: Freud proposed that human behavior is driven by two opposing major instincts. One of these pushes us toward survival, reproduction and keeping life going. Which of the following correctly describes this instinct, called eros?

dw.The psychic energy, or sex drive, that f: That is libido, the energy that fuels eros.

bank.q: What is libido?
bank.a: The psychic energy, or sex drive, that fuels the life instinct
d: The major instinct that aims to preserve and perpetuate life
A part of the body that is sensitive to sexual stimulation
The automatic ejection of anxiety-evoking ideas from awareness
bank.why: Freud called the energy of eros libido; it is psychosexual.
dh: The psychic energy, or sex drive, that fuels the death instinct
The life instinct itself, which aims to preserve and perpetuate life
The psychic energy, or moral drive, that fuels the superego
bank.xq: Freud believed that the life instinct needs a source of energy to drive it, and he gave that energy a special name. Which statement correctly describes libido and its relationship to the life instinct?

dw.The major instinct that aims to preserve: That is eros, the life instinct itself; libido is its energy.
dw.A part of the body that is sensitive to: That is an erogenous zone, a body part.
dw.The automatic ejection of anxiety-evokin: That is repression, a defense mechanism.

bank.q: What is an erogenous zone?
bank.a: A body part where libidinal energy is expressed in a given stage
d: The psychic energy, or sex drive, that fuels the life instinct
Excessive or insufficient gratification in a stage of development
The conflict in which a child desires the parent of the other gender
bank.why: Development moves libido from one erogenous zone to another: mouth, anus, phallic region, genitals.
dh: A body part where libidinal energy is repressed in a given stage
A stage of life in which libidinal energy becomes fixated
A body part where the moral energy of the superego is expressed
bank.xq: In Freud's theory of development, the mouth is important in infancy, the anus in toddlerhood and the genitals in early childhood, because pleasure is centered on a different part of the body at each stage. Which statement correctly describes such a body part?

dw.The psychic energy, or sex drive, that f: That is libido, the energy, not the body part.

bank.q: In psychosexual development, what is fixation?
bank.a: Getting stuck in a stage from too much or too little gratification
d: Moving libidinal energy from one erogenous zone to the next
Repressing sexual urges and preferring same-gender playmates
Identifying with the same-gender parent to resolve a rivalry
bank.why: Fixation leads to traits typical of the stage, such as oral dependency.
dh: Getting stuck in a stage only from too little gratification
Moving to the next stage early from too much or too little gratification
Getting stuck in a stage from too much or too little punishment
