bank.xq: One adult whose infant feeding needs were neglected and another whose every need was instantly indulged may both, Freud said, carry traits from that early stage into adulthood. In Freud's psychosexual theory, what is this getting stuck called and what causes it?

dw.Moving libidinal energy from one erogeno: That is normal development: libido moving between zones.
dw.Identifying with the same-gender parent: That is identification, which resolves the Oedipus or Electra complex.

bank.q: What is the order of Freud's psychosexual stages?
bank.a: Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital
d: Oral, phallic, anal, latency, genital
Anal, oral, phallic, genital, latency
Oral, anal, latency, phallic, genital
bank.why: Oral (0–1), anal (2nd year), phallic (3–6), latency (5 or 6 to puberty), genital (puberty on).
bank.xq: Freud proposed that personality develops through five psychosexual stages as libido shifts to different erogenous zones from infancy through adulthood. Which choice lists these stages in the correct order?

dw.Anal, oral, phallic, genital, latency: Oral comes first, and latency comes before genital.
dw.Oral, anal, latency, phallic, genital: Latency comes after phallic, not before.

bank.q: Marisa is five months old and always chews her rattle. According to Freud, she is in the ____ stage.
bank.a: Oral
d: Anal
Phallic
Latency
bank.why: During the first year, gratification comes mainly through sucking and biting.
bank.hint: If it fits, into the mouth it goes.
bank.xq: Marisa is five months old. Whatever she gets her hands on, especially her rattle, goes straight into her mouth, and she seems to get great pleasure from sucking and chewing on it. According to Freud, in which psychosexual stage is Marisa?

dw.Anal: Anal is about the second year (toilet training).
dw.Latency: Latency runs from about 5 or 6 to puberty.

bank.q: An adult smokes, overeats, bites his nails and wants clinging, dependent relationships. Freud would trace this to which stage?
bank.a: Oral
d: Anal
Phallic
Genital
bank.why: Oral fixation: dependency, gullibility, smoking, overeating. (The book adds that research does not support this.)
bank.xq: A middle-aged man is a heavy smoker, often overeats, bites his nails when nervous, and tends to form clinging, dependent relationships with the people around him. Freud would say his adult traits come from fixation at which psychosexual stage?

dw.Anal: Anal fixation shows as control traits (neat or messy), not dependency.
dw.Phallic: Phallic fixation belongs to the Oedipus and Electra stage, not smoking and overeating.
dw.Genital: Genital is the mature stage at puberty; this pattern is oral.

bank.q: A coworker is a perfectionist with a strong need for order, neatness and cleanliness. In Freud's terms these are ____ traits.
bank.a: Anal-retentive
d: Anal-expulsive
Oral
Phallic
bank.why: Anal-retentive traits come from excessive self-control: perfectionism, order, neatness.
bank.xq: A coworker reorganizes her desk several times a day, cannot stand a single item out of place, and insists that every report be perfect and spotless. According to Freud's theory of fixation during toilet training, what are these traits called?

dw.Anal-expulsive: Anal-expulsive is the messy, careless type.
dw.Oral: Oral traits are dependency and smoking, not neatness.
dw.Phallic: Phallic is the stage of the Oedipus and Electra complexes, not toilet-training control.

bank.q: A roommate is careless and messy and seems to enjoy others' discomfort. Freud would call these ____ traits.
bank.a: Anal-expulsive
d: Anal-retentive
Oral
Latency
bank.why: Anal-expulsive traits “let it all hang out”: carelessness, messiness, even sadism.
bank.xq: Your roommate leaves dishes and clothes everywhere, never cleans up, and even seems to enjoy watching others get annoyed by the mess. According to Freud's theory of fixation during toilet training, how would these traits be described?

dw.Anal-retentive: Anal-retentive is the neat, orderly perfectionist.
dw.Oral: Oral traits are dependency, smoking and overeating.
dw.Latency: Latency is the quiet stage with no sexual focus; carelessness and messiness are anal-expulsive.

bank.q: What is the Oedipus complex?
bank.a: A boy's wish to possess his mother, with the father seen as a rival
d: A girl's longing for her father and resentment of her mother
The repression of all sexual urges between age 6 and puberty
Excessive self-control learned during toilet training
bank.why: It arises in the phallic stage and is resolved by about age 5 or 6 through identification with the father.
dh: A boy's wish to possess his father, with the mother seen as a rival
A girl's wish to possess her mother, with the father seen as a rival
A girl's wish to possess her father, with the mother seen as a rival
bank.xq: In the phallic stage, Freud said a young child develops a strong attachment to one parent and sees the other parent as competition. Freud named one version of this conflict after a Greek king who unknowingly killed his father and married his mother. Which of the following correctly describes the Oedipus complex?

dw.The repression of all sexual urges betwe: That is latency, not the Oedipus complex.

bank.q: What is the Electra complex?
bank.a: A girl's longing for her father and resentment of her mother
d: A boy's wish to possess his mother, with the father seen as a rival
A drive for superiority that grows out of feeling small
The redirection of sexual urges onto partners outside the family
bank.why: Electra, daughter of King Agamemnon, longed for her father after his death.
dh: A girl's longing for her mother and resentment of her father
A boy's longing for his mother and resentment of his father
A boy's longing for his father and resentment of his mother
bank.xq: Freud's account of the phallic stage includes a conflict that is the female counterpart of the Oedipus complex, named after a figure in Greek tragedy. Which of the following correctly describes this Electra complex?

dw.A drive for superiority that grows out o: That is Adler's inferiority complex and drive for superiority.
dw.The redirection of sexual urges onto par: That is the genital stage at puberty.

bank.q: How are the Oedipus and Electra complexes resolved?
bank.a: By identifying with the parent of the same gender
d: By marrying someone who resembles the other parent
By remaining fixated in the phallic stage
By sublimating the urges into schoolwork during the genital stage
bank.why: Children repress hostility toward the same-gender parent and identify with that parent; identification is the key to gender-typing.
dh: By identifying with the parent of the other gender
By repressing the wish and identifying with the parent of the other gender
By identifying with peers of the same gender during the latency stage
bank.xq: Freud believed that a child in the phallic stage eventually stops seeing one parent as a rival and lets go of the forbidden wish for the other parent, taking on the gender role and values of that rival parent instead. How, according to Freud, are the Oedipus and Electra complexes resolved?

dw.By marrying someone who resembles the ot: Freud did not describe it that way; the child identifies with the same-gender parent.
dw.By remaining fixated in the phallic stag: Fixation is a failure of development, not how the conflict is resolved.
dw.By sublimating the urges into schoolwork: Channeling urges into schoolwork is latency, which follows identification.

bank.q: An eight-year-old prefers playmates of his own gender, has no conscious sexual interests and focuses on schoolwork. Which stage is this?
bank.a: Latency
d: Phallic
Genital
Anal
bank.why: In latency, sexual feelings stay unconscious and libido is channeled into socially acceptable activity.
bank.xq: An eight-year-old boy plays only with other boys, shows no conscious interest in sexual matters, and spends most of his energy on schoolwork and sports. According to Freud, which psychosexual stage best describes this period of his life?

dw.Phallic: Phallic (3 to 6) is when the Oedipus and Electra complexes arise.
dw.Genital: Genital begins at puberty, when sexual interests reawaken.
dw.Anal: Anal is the second year of life.

bank.q: When does the genital stage begin?
bank.a: At puberty
d: At about age 3
In the second year of life
At about age 5 or 6
bank.why: Sexual urges reawaken at puberty and are displaced onto socially appropriate partners.
bank.xq: In Freud's last psychosexual stage, sexual impulses reawaken after a period of dormancy, and the person begins to seek mature sexual relationships with people outside the family. When does this genital stage begin?

dw.At about age 3: About age 3 is when the phallic stage begins.
dw.In the second year of life: The second year is the anal stage.
dw.At about age 5 or 6: Ages 5 or 6 mark the start of latency.

bank.q: The phallic stage, when the Oedipus and Electra complexes arise, covers about which ages?
bank.a: 3 to 6 years
d: Birth to 1 year
The second year
Puberty onward
bank.why: The phallic stage starts in the third year; the complexes are resolved by about 5 or 6.
dh: 2 to 3 years
6 years to puberty
1 to 3 years
bank.xq: Freud believed that the Oedipus and Electra complexes arise during the phallic stage, when the child's pleasure is focused on the genitals. About what ages does the phallic stage cover?

dw.Birth to 1 year: Birth to 1 year is the oral stage.
dw.The second year: The second year is the anal stage.
dw.Puberty onward: Puberty onward is the genital stage.

bank.q: What did Jung mean by the collective unconscious?
bank.a: A store of primitive images, or archetypes, that reflects the history of the species
d: The part of the mind holding primitive instincts and repressed urges kept out of awareness
Feelings of inferiority that drive people to seek superiority
The part of the mind holding ideas that can be made conscious by focusing on them
bank.why: Jung added it to the personal unconscious. Archetypes include the hero, the nurturing mother and the wise old man.
dh: A store of primitive images, or archetypes, that reflects one person's repressed history
A store of repressed urges that reflects the history of the species
A store of learned images, or schemas, that reflects one's own culture
bank.xq: Carl Jung noticed that similar symbols, such as the wise old man, the great mother and the hero, appear in the myths and dreams of people from many different cultures who have never met. Which statement correctly describes the concept Jung proposed to explain this?

dw.The part of the mind holding primitive i: That is Freud's unconscious, which is personal.

bank.q: Which neo-Freudian developed analytical psychology and downplayed sex as just one of several instincts?
bank.a: Carl Jung
d: Alfred Adler
Karen Horney
Erik Erikson
bank.why: Jung was in Freud's inner circle until he developed his own theory.
bank.xq: One of Freud's followers broke away from him because he felt Freud placed too much emphasis on sexual impulses. This theorist treated sex as just one of several instincts and called his own theory analytical psychology. Who is this neo-Freudian?

dw.Alfred Adler: Adler developed individual psychology and the inferiority complex.
dw.Karen Horney: Horney stressed social relationships and challenged Freud's view of women.

bank.q: Who believed people are motivated by an inferiority complex that gives rise to a drive for superiority?
bank.a: Alfred Adler
d: Carl Jung
Karen Horney
Sigmund Freud
bank.why: Adler, who had rickets as a child, called his theory individual psychology.
bank.xq: A neo-Freudian argued that people are driven not mainly by sex, but by feelings of being smaller or weaker than others, which push them to strive to become better and more capable. Who believed people are motivated by an inferiority complex that gives rise to a drive for superiority?

dw.Carl Jung: Jung developed analytical psychology and the collective unconscious.
dw.Karen Horney: Horney argued against penis envy and stressed culture and relationships.
dw.Sigmund Freud: Freud stressed sex and the unconscious, not an inferiority complex.

bank.q: In Adler's theory, what is the creative self?
bank.a: The self-aware part of personality that strives to reach its potential
d: A store of primitive images that reflects the history of the species
The structure that uses reason to satisfy the id while avoiding disapproval
A firm sense of who one is and what one stands for in life
bank.why: Because each person's potential is unique, Adler's views are called individual psychology.
dh: The unconscious part of personality that strives to reach its potential
The self-aware part of personality that strives to overcome the superego
The self-aware part of personality that strives to satisfy the id
bank.xq: Alfred Adler believed that people are not merely pushed by unconscious drives but are aware of themselves and actively shape their own lives toward growth. Which statement correctly describes what Adler called the creative self?

bank.q: Karen Horney disagreed with Freud mainly because she argued that
bank.a: girls do not feel inferior to boys; social relationships matter more than sex
d: the collective unconscious matters more than the personal unconscious in shaping adult personality
the id develops before birth, so instincts are fixed earlier than Freud said
personality is shaped only by reinforcement and has no unconscious part
bank.why: Horney said ideas like penis envy came from Western cultural prejudice; she believed consistent love can undo a traumatic childhood.
dh: girls do feel inferior to boys, but social relationships matter more than sex
girls do not feel inferior to boys, but sex matters more than social relationships
girls feel inferior to boys, and sex matters more than social relationships
bank.xq: Karen Horney was trained in psychoanalysis, but she rejected parts of Freud's theory, especially his view of women and of what drives personality. Which statement best captures her main disagreement with Freud?

dw.the collective unconscious matters more: That is Jung's emphasis, not Horney's.
dw.the id develops before birth, so instinc: Horney did not argue about when the id develops; her objection was to penis envy and to sex as the main driver.
dw.personality is shaped only by reinforcem: Reinforcement-only is the behaviorist view; Horney kept the unconscious.

bank.q: How did Erikson's theory differ from Freud's?
bank.a: He proposed psychosocial stages, with ego identity as the goal of adolescence
d: He proposed psychosexual stages named after the body's erogenous zones
He replaced the personal unconscious with a collective unconscious
He argued that personality is completely fixed by about age 5 or 6
bank.why: Erikson thought social relationships matter more than sexual urges and that we are largely the architects of our personalities.
dh: He proposed psychosexual stages, with ego identity as the goal of adolescence
He proposed psychosocial stages, with ego identity as the goal of early childhood
He proposed psychosocial stages, with intimacy as the goal of adolescence
bank.xq: Erik Erikson, like Freud, described personality as developing in stages, but his stages extend across the whole life span and focus on a different kind of challenge. Which statement correctly describes how Erikson's theory differed from Freud's?

dw.He proposed psychosexual stages named af: That is Freud's theory; Erikson's stages are psychosocial.
dw.He replaced the personal unconscious wit: The collective unconscious is Jung's idea.
dw.He argued that personality is completely: Freud, not Erikson, said personality is fixed in early childhood; Erikson's stages span life.

bank.q: Which is a main criticism of the psychodynamic perspective?
bank.a: Its concepts are too vague to test, and it rests mostly on case studies
d: It ignores the effects of early childhood experiences on adults
It explains personality only through rewards and punishments
It describes traits without saying where those traits come from
bank.why: Critics also call Freud's views of women sexist; strengths include stressing childhood and the unconscious.
dh: Its concepts are easy to test, but it rests mostly on laboratory animals
Its concepts are too vague to test, and it rests mostly on large surveys
Its concepts are precise, but it rests mostly on case studies
bank.xq: Critics of the psychodynamic perspective point out that ideas such as the id and the Oedipus complex cannot be observed directly, and that Freud built his theory largely on his own patients. Which statement best summarizes a main criticism of this perspective?

dw.It ignores the effects of early childhoo: The opposite: psychodynamic theory stresses early childhood.
dw.It explains personality only through rew: That describes behaviorism, not psychodynamic theory.
dw.It describes traits without saying where: That is a criticism of trait theory.

bank.q: Who are the neo-Freudians?
bank.a: Freud's followers who kept inner conflict but stressed social factors
d: Theorists who replaced the unconscious with observable behavior only and measurable responses
Trait theorists who used factor analysis to find basic traits
Existentialists who saw human life as trivial and without meaning
bank.why: Jung, Adler, Horney and Erikson kept conflict and defense mechanisms but put less weight on sex.
dh: Freud's followers who kept inner conflict and stressed sexual factors even more
Freud's followers who dropped inner conflict and stressed social factors
Freud's critics who dropped the unconscious and stressed observable behavior
bank.xq: Jung, Adler, Horney and Erikson were all influenced by Freud, but each changed his theory in important ways, especially regarding what drives personality. Which statement best describes who the neo-Freudians are?

bank.q: What is a trait?
bank.a: A relatively stable element of personality that is inferred from behavior
d: A pattern of behavior learned through reinforcement in one situation
A store of primitive images shared by the species
A belief that one can accomplish a certain task
bank.why: Traits are assumed to explain consistent behavior across situations, such as a shy friend staying quiet at most parties.
dh: A relatively unstable element of personality that changes with each situation
A relatively stable element of personality that is directly observed, not inferred
A relatively stable element of the unconscious that is inferred from dreams
bank.xq: When we say a friend is "friendly" or "honest," we are not describing a single act but a lasting quality we have figured out from watching how she acts over time and across situations. Which statement best describes what psychologists mean by a trait?

dw.A pattern of behavior learned through re: That is a learned behavior, the behaviorist view, not a stable trait.

bank.q: In Hippocrates' theory, an excess of yellow bile gives which temperament?
bank.a: Choleric (quick-tempered)
d: Sanguine (warm, cheerful)
Phlegmatic (sluggish, calm)
Melancholic (gloomy, pensive)
bank.why: Yellow bile = choleric.
bank.xq: The ancient Greek physician Hippocrates believed that personality depends on the balance of four bodily fluids, or humors. A person with an excess of yellow bile was thought to have which temperament?

bank.q: In Hippocrates' theory, which fluid goes with a sanguine (warm, cheerful) temperament?
bank.a: Blood
d: Phlegm
Yellow bile
Black bile
bank.why: Blood = sanguine.
bank.hint: Think of the Latin root of “sanguine.”
bank.xq: In Hippocrates' theory of the four humors, each bodily fluid matches a temperament. A person who is warm, cheerful and lively was believed to have an excess of which fluid?

bank.q: Which humor was linked with a melancholic temperament and with depression?
bank.a: Black bile
d: Yellow bile
Phlegm
Blood
bank.why: An excess of black bile was thought to cause depression; bloodletting and vomiting were used to restore balance.
bank.xq: In Hippocrates' theory, one of the four humors was linked with a gloomy, pensive temperament, and the name of that temperament is still connected with depression today. Which humor was this?

bank.q: A sluggish, calm, cool person would be called ____ in Hippocrates' scheme.
bank.a: Phlegmatic
d: Choleric
Sanguine
Melancholic
bank.why: Phlegm = phlegmatic.
bank.xq: A classmate is slow-moving, calm, cool and rarely gets excited about anything, even under pressure. Using Hippocrates' scheme of four temperaments, how would this person be described?

bank.q: Gordon Allport and a colleague cataloged about how many human traits from word lists such as dictionaries?
bank.a: About 18,000
d: About 5
About 180
About 1,800
bank.why: Physical, behavioral and moral traits; the list became the base for later research.
bank.xq: Gordon Allport and a colleague tried to list every human trait by going through word lists such as dictionaries and noting every word that could describe a personality. About how many traits did they catalog?

dw.About 5: Five is the number of the Big Five factors, not the traits Allport cataloged.
dw.About 180: Still too few; the list ran to about 18,000.
dw.About 1,800: Ten times too few; the list ran to about 18,000.

bank.q: Hans Eysenck described personality mainly with which two dimensions?
bank.a: Introversion–extraversion and stability–instability
d: Agreeableness–hostility and openness–shallowness as the two basic poles
Id versus superego, with the ego as the go-between
Internal versus external locus of control
bank.why: Emotional instability is also called neuroticism.
dh: Introversion–extraversion and openness–shallowness
Agreeableness–hostility and stability–instability
Conscientiousness–carelessness and introversion–extraversion
bank.xq: Hans Eysenck reduced the many traits found by earlier researchers to a small number of basic dimensions and used them to explain Hippocrates' four temperaments. Which two dimensions did Eysenck mainly use to describe personality?

dw.Agreeableness–hostility and openness–sha: Those are Big Five style dimensions, not Eysenck's two.
dw.Id versus superego, with the ego as the: That is Freud's structure, not a trait dimension.
dw.Internal versus external locus of contro: Locus of control is a social-cognitive concept, not Eysenck's.

bank.q: Emotional instability is also called
bank.a: neuroticism
d: introversion
psychoticism
agreeableness
bank.why: Eysenck's emotional stability–instability dimension; neuroticism is also one of the Big Five.
bank.xq: In Eysenck's two-dimensional model, one dimension runs from people who are calm and even-tempered to people who are anxious, moody and easily upset. What is the unstable end of this dimension also called?

dw.introversion: Introversion is the opposite of extraversion, a different dimension.
dw.psychoticism: Psychoticism is a separate dimension, not another name for instability.
dw.agreeableness: Agreeableness is a Big Five factor, not instability.

bank.q: What is introversion?
bank.a: A tendency toward intense imagination and holding impulses in
d: A tendency to be socially outgoing and to express feelings freely
A tendency to be nervous, moody and sensitive to negative events
A tendency to be organized, thorough and reliable
bank.why: Extraversion is the opposite: outgoing and freely expressive.
dh: A tendency toward intense imagination and expressing impulses freely
A tendency toward social outgoingness and holding impulses in
A tendency toward emotional instability and holding impulses in
bank.xq: In Eysenck's model, one end of a basic personality dimension describes people who are imaginative and who tend to keep their impulses in check. Which statement correctly describes introversion?

bank.q: What is extraversion?
bank.a: A tendency to be socially outgoing and to express feelings freely
d: A tendency toward intense imagination and holding impulses in check
A tendency to be kind, trusting and warm
A tendency to be imaginative, curious and creative
bank.why: Carl Jung was the first to distinguish introverts from extraverts.
dh: A tendency to be socially outgoing but to hold feelings in
A tendency to be socially withdrawn but to express feelings freely
A tendency to be emotionally unstable and to express feelings freely
bank.xq: In Eysenck's model, the other end of that same dimension describes people who enjoy being with others and say what they feel without holding back. Which statement correctly describes extraversion?

bank.q: In Eysenck's scheme, an extraverted and emotionally unstable person matches which of Hippocrates' types?
bank.a: Choleric
d: Sanguine
Phlegmatic
Melancholic
bank.why: Extraverted + unstable = choleric; extraverted + stable = sanguine; introverted + stable = phlegmatic; introverted + unstable = melancholic.
bank.xq: Eysenck showed how his two dimensions match Hippocrates' four temperaments. A person who is highly sociable and outgoing but is also emotionally unstable and easily upset would fit which of Hippocrates' types?

bank.q: An introverted and emotionally stable person matches which type?
bank.a: Phlegmatic
d: Melancholic
Choleric
Sanguine
bank.why: Introverted + stable = phlegmatic (calm, careful, even-tempered).
bank.xq: Using Eysenck's two dimensions to map Hippocrates' four types, a person who is quiet and inward-looking but also calm and emotionally stable would match which temperament?

bank.q: In Eysenck's terms, an anxious person would be
bank.a: high in introversion and high in neuroticism
d: high in extraversion and low in neuroticism, a calm and outgoing type
low in introversion and high in stability
high in openness and agreeableness
bank.why: Anxious: preoccupied with one's own thoughts (introverted) and emotionally unstable.
dh: high in extraversion and high in neuroticism
high in introversion and low in neuroticism
low in introversion and low in neuroticism
bank.xq: A student worries constantly, keeps to herself, and rarely shares her feelings with others, and she is easily upset by small setbacks. Using Eysenck's two dimensions, how would an anxious person like her be described?

dw.high in extraversion and low in neurotic: That is the opposite: an extraverted, stable person.
dw.low in introversion and high in stabilit: Low introversion and high stability describes a calm extravert.
dw.high in openness and agreeableness: Openness and agreeableness are Big Five factors, not Eysenck's anxiety pattern.

bank.q: Which list gives the Big Five personality factors?
bank.a: Extraversion, neuroticism, conscientiousness, agreeableness, openness
d: Extraversion, psychoticism, conscientiousness, agreeableness, openness
Narcissism, neuroticism, conscientiousness, agreeableness, openness
Depression, obsessiveness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, openness
bank.why: Remember OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism.
bank.xq: Many researchers now believe that personality can be summarized by five broad factors that appear across many cultures and tests. Which list correctly gives these Big Five personality factors?

dw.Extraversion, psychoticism, conscientiou: Psychoticism is Eysenck's dimension, not a Big Five factor.
dw.Narcissism, neuroticism, conscientiousne: Narcissism is not a Big Five factor.
dw.Depression, obsessiveness, conscientious: Depression and obsessiveness are not Big Five factors.

bank.q: Which theorists played a key role in the five-factor model?
bank.a: Robert McCrae and Paul Costa
d: Hans and Sybil Eysenck
Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan
Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert
bank.why: They also built the NEO Five-Factor Inventory to measure the factors.
bank.xq: The five-factor model of personality is supported by research in many cultures and is measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory. Which theorists played a key role in developing this model?

dw.Hans and Sybil Eysenck: The Eysencks built a two-dimension model.
dw.Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan: Murray and Morgan created the TAT.
dw.Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert: Allport and Odbert cataloged trait words.

bank.q: Kindness, trust and warmth versus hostility, selfishness and distrust describes which Big Five factor?
bank.a: Agreeableness
d: Conscientiousness
Extraversion
Openness to experience
bank.why: Agreeable people even get fewer traffic citations and accidents.
bank.xq: One Big Five factor ranges from people who are kind, trusting and warm toward others to people who are hostile, selfish and distrustful. Which Big Five factor does this describe?

bank.q: Organization, thoroughness and reliability versus carelessness and negligence describes which factor?
bank.a: Conscientiousness
d: Agreeableness and warmth
Neuroticism
Extraversion
bank.why: Political conservatives tend to score higher on it.
bank.xq: One Big Five factor describes how people approach their duties. At one end are people who are organized, thorough and reliable, and at the other end are people who are careless and negligent. Which factor is this?

bank.q: Imagination, curiosity and creativity versus shallowness describes which factor?
bank.a: Openness to experience
d: Extraversion
Conscientiousness
Agreeableness
bank.why: Political liberals tend to score higher on openness.
bank.xq: A student loves trying new foods, is curious about other cultures, and enjoys making art and imagining new ideas, while a classmate prefers the familiar and shows little curiosity. Which Big Five factor separates these two people?

bank.q: What does research suggest about the biology of extraversion?
bank.a: About 40–60% heritable; extraverts have more brain dopamine
d: It is learned entirely from parents through reinforcement alone
It depends on the balance of the four bodily humors
It is set by the superego during early childhood
bank.why: Genetic factors are also part of a child's temperament, such as shyness and behavioral inhibition.
dh: About 40–60% heritable; extraverts have less brain dopamine
About 10–20% heritable; extraverts have more brain dopamine
About 80–90% heritable; extraverts have more brain serotonin
bank.xq: Studies of twins and of brain chemistry have been used to explore whether extraversion has a biological basis. Which statement best summarizes what research suggests about the biology of extraversion?

dw.It is learned entirely from parents thro: Research shows a large genetic part, so it is not learned entirely.
dw.It depends on the balance of the four bo: The humors are Hippocrates' old theory, not research findings.
dw.It is set by the superego during early c: The superego is Freud's concept, not a basis for extraversion.

bank.q: Adrian Raine linked the antisocial personality to impairments in which brain areas?
bank.a: The ventral prefrontal cortex and the amygdala
d: The occipital lobe and the cerebellum
Broca's area and Wernicke's area
The medulla and the pons of the hindbrain
bank.why: Antisocial people show low emotional response to threats and little guilt or anxiety.
dh: The ventral prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus
The occipital cortex and the amygdala
The dorsal parietal cortex and the hypothalamus
bank.xq: Adrian Raine studied the brains of people with antisocial personality, who often show little guilt or fear of punishment. He linked this personality to impairments in which brain areas?

dw.The occipital lobe and the cerebellum: Those areas handle vision and movement, not emotion and conscience.
dw.The medulla and the pons of the hindbrai: Those hindbrain areas handle basic life functions.

bank.q: What is a main limitation of trait theory?
bank.a: It describes traits but does not explain their origins
d: It depends on unconscious structures that cannot be measured
It ignores personality tests and job matching completely
It denies that any traits are inherited
bank.why: Its strength: it led to personality tests and to matching people with jobs.
dh: It explains the origins of traits but cannot describe them
It describes traits but cannot measure them with tests
It describes traits but denies that they are stable
bank.xq: Trait theory is useful for describing people, for example by saying someone is highly conscientious and low in neuroticism. However, critics say it leaves an important question unanswered. What is a main limitation of trait theory?

dw.It depends on unconscious structures tha: That is a criticism of psychodynamic theory.
dw.It ignores personality tests and job mat: The opposite: trait theory led to personality tests and job matching.
dw.It denies that any traits are inherited: The opposite: trait theory assumes traits are inherited.

bank.q: Which is an assumption of most modern trait theories?
bank.a: Traits are inherited and embedded in the nervous system
d: Traits are flexible and change with each new situation or social setting
Traits are learned mainly by imitating parents
Traits come from fixation in the psychosexual stages
bank.why: They also rely on factor analysis, developed by Spearman, to find which traits are basic.
dh: Traits are learned and embedded in the nervous system
Traits are inherited and embedded in the unconscious mind
Traits are inherited but change with every new situation
bank.xq: Unlike older views that described traits only in terms of behavior, most modern trait theories make an assumption about where traits come from and where they reside. Which statement reflects this assumption?

dw.Traits are flexible and change with each: Traits are seen as stable, not changing with each situation.
dw.Traits are learned mainly by imitating p: Imitation is social-cognitive learning, not the trait view.

bank.q: Watson's claim that he could train any of “a dozen healthy infants” to become any type of specialist expresses the view that
bank.a: personality is plastic and shaped by the environment
d: personality is fixed by inherited traits
personality comes from unconscious conflicts
personality depends on self-actualization
bank.why: Behaviorists saw situational influences, not inner variables, as the shapers of personality.
dh: personality is plastic and shaped by inner choice
personality is fixed early and shaped by the environment only in infancy
personality is plastic and shaped by inherited traits
bank.xq: John B. Watson claimed that if he were given "a dozen healthy infants," he could train any one of them to become a doctor, a lawyer or even a thief, regardless of the child's talents or ancestry. What view of personality does this famous claim express?

dw.personality is fixed by inherited traits: That is the trait view; Watson stressed the environment.

bank.q: The views of Watson and Skinner largely ignore the notion of
bank.a: personal freedom and choice
d: environmental variables
reinforcement and punishment
shaping
bank.why: Skinner said to avoid looking into the “black box” and to study the effects of reinforcement.
bank.xq: Watson and Skinner explained behavior almost entirely in terms of rewards, punishments and other environmental influences. Critics argue that this left something important about human beings out of their theories. Which notion do the views of Watson and Skinner largely ignore?

dw.reinforcement and punishment: Reinforcement and punishment were central to Skinner.

bank.q: In Skinner's novel Walden Two, people are content because
bank.a: they were conditioned from childhood to want to cooperate
d: they freely chose to strive toward self-actualization
they had resolved their Oedipus and Electra complexes
they were born with highly agreeable personality traits and needed no learning
bank.why: They see themselves as free, but their reinforcement histories shaped what they want.
dh: they were conditioned as adults to want to cooperate
they freely chose as children to want to cooperate
they were conditioned from childhood to want to compete
bank.xq: B. F. Skinner wrote a novel, Walden Two, describing a community where people live together happily and work well with one another. According to the novel, why are the people in this community content?

dw.they freely chose to strive toward self-: Free choice toward self-actualization is the humanistic view; Walden Two relies on conditioning.
dw.they had resolved their Oedipus and Elec: Oedipus and Electra complexes are Freud's, not Skinner's.
dw.they were born with highly agreeable per: Born-with traits are the trait view; Skinner stressed reinforcement.

bank.q: What is social cognitive theory?
bank.a: A learning theory stressing observation and person variables
d: A theory that personality is shaped by rewards and punishments alone
A theory that personality consists of five largely inherited factors
A theory that personality reflects the balance of id, ego and superego
bank.why: Developed by Albert Bandura.
dh: A learning theory stressing reinforcement and ignoring person variables
A trait theory stressing observation and person variables
A learning theory stressing observation and situational variables only
bank.xq: Albert Bandura agreed that people learn from rewards and punishments, but he added that they also learn by watching others and that their own thoughts and expectations shape what they do. Which statement correctly describes his social cognitive theory?

dw.A theory that personality is shaped by r: That is behaviorism; social cognitive theory adds observation and person variables.
dw.A theory that personality consists of fi: That is trait theory (the Big Five).

bank.q: Social cognitive theory differs from behaviorism in arguing that
bank.a: people influence their environment as it influences them
d: rewards and punishments are what shape behavior
wants and desires come only from the environment
the ego follows the moral principle, not reality
bank.why: It keeps observable behavior but adds person variables.
dh: the environment influences people, but people do not influence it
people influence their environment, but it does not influence them
people and their environment do not influence each other
bank.xq: A behaviorist would say a child becomes aggressive because aggression is rewarded at home. A social cognitive theorist would add that the child's aggression also changes how others treat him, which in turn shapes him further. In what way does social cognitive theory differ from behaviorism?

dw.wants and desires come only from the env: That is the behaviorist view; social cognitive theory says people shape their environment too.
dw.the ego follows the moral principle, not: That mixes up Freud's structures; the moral principle belongs to the superego and has nothing to do with this question.

bank.q: In social cognitive theory, which is a person variable rather than a situational variable?
bank.a: Expectancies about outcomes
d: Rewards given for the behavior
Punishments that follow it
The setting the person is in
bank.why: Person variables: knowledge and skills, ways of interpreting experience, expectancies, emotions, self-regulatory plans.
bank.xq: Social cognitive theorists separate situational variables, which come from the person's surroundings, from person variables, which come from within the person, such as beliefs and ways of thinking. Which of the following is a person variable rather than a situational variable?

dw.The setting the person is in: The setting is a situational variable.

bank.q: What are self-efficacy expectations?
bank.a: Beliefs that we can accomplish certain things
d: Beliefs about what will follow what in other people's behavior
Standards by which the value of a person is judged
Impressions of ourselves and evaluations of our adequacy
bank.why: Positive self-efficacy goes with high self-esteem and achievement motivation.
dh: Beliefs that others can accomplish certain things for us
Beliefs about what rewards will follow certain behaviors
Beliefs that our worth depends on accomplishing certain things
bank.xq: Before a big presentation, one student thinks, "I can do this; I've prepared and I'm capable," while another thinks, "I'll never be able to pull this off." In social cognitive theory, these beliefs about one's own ability are examples of what?

dw.Beliefs about what will follow what in o: That describes outcome expectancies, not beliefs about your own ability.

bank.q: Lisa is studying musical theater and is convinced that if she works hard enough she will make it to Broadway. Her conviction is an example of
bank.a: self-efficacy expectations
d: competencies and skills they have learned
observational modeling
encoding strategies
bank.why: A belief in one's ability to accomplish something.
bank.xq: Lisa is studying musical theater. Despite stiff competition, she is convinced that if she keeps working hard enough, she will be able to make it all the way to Broadway. In social cognitive terms, her conviction is an example of

dw.competencies and skills they have learne: Competencies and skills are what she can actually do, not her belief about it.
dw.observational modeling: Observational modeling is learning by watching others.
dw.encoding strategies: Encoding strategies are how people interpret and store experiences.

bank.q: In social cognitive theory, what is observational learning?
bank.a: Learning by watching others, without acting or being reinforced
d: Learning a response because it was directly reinforced each time
Learning to link two stimuli because they were paired repeatedly
Learning that stays hidden until a reward makes it appear
bank.why: Also called modeling or cognitive learning; reading about others counts too.
dh: Learning by watching others, but only after being reinforced for it
Learning by acting and being reinforced, without watching others
Learning by watching others, which always shows up right away in behavior
bank.xq: A child watches his older sister get scolded for touching the stove and, without ever touching it himself or being punished, learns to stay away from it. He may not even show what he learned until much later. In social cognitive theory, which statement describes this kind of learning?

dw.Learning a response because it was direc: That is operant learning: direct reinforcement.
dw.Learning that stays hidden until a rewar: That is latent learning, not learning by watching.

bank.q: Which is a criticism of the learning perspectives on personality?
bank.a: They play down consciousness, choice, self-awareness and genes
d: They rely on inner structures that cannot be seen or measured
They ignore the effects of the environment on behavior
They describe traits without explaining where traits come from
bank.why: Their strength: insisting on observable behavior and showing how reinforcement and observation shape us.
dh: They play up consciousness, choice, self-awareness and genes
They play down the environment, rewards and punishments
They play down consciousness and choice but overstate genes
bank.xq: Learning theorists explain personality mainly in terms of experiences in the environment and what people learn from them. Critics argue that this view leaves out important parts of what makes us human. Which statement describes a common criticism of the learning perspectives on personality?

dw.They rely on inner structures that canno: That is a criticism of psychodynamic theory.
dw.They ignore the effects of the environme: The opposite: learning perspectives stress the environment.
dw.They describe traits without explaining: That is a criticism of trait theory.

bank.q: What is gender-typing?
bank.a: Coming to show behavior patterns that fit stereotypical gender roles
d: One's psychological sense of being female, male or in between
Blending self-esteem with how one fits the culture's gender roles in daily life
The direction of one's romantic and erotic attractions
bank.why: Biology (prenatal hormones) and social learning both contribute.
dh: Coming to show behavior patterns that defy stereotypical gender roles
One's psychological sense of fitting stereotypical gender roles
Being assigned stereotypical gender roles at birth
bank.xq: By age five, a girl insists on playing with dolls and wearing pink, while her brother prefers trucks and rough play, both acting in the ways their culture expects of girls and boys. Which statement correctly describes this process, called gender-typing?

dw.Blending self-esteem with how one fits t: That mixes self-esteem with gender roles; it is not the definition of gender-typing.

bank.q: What is gender-schema theory?
bank.a: The view that children who know their sex try to live up to gender-typed traits
d: The view that children imitate same-gender models because they are rewarded
The view that gender differences were shaped by natural selection
The view that gender-typing comes from resolving the Oedipus complex
bank.why: Gender becomes important because society emphasizes it.
dh: The view that children who know their sex are rewarded into gender-typed traits
The view that children try to live up to gender-typed traits before they know their sex
The view that children who know their sex inherit gender-typed traits
bank.xq: Sandra Bem proposed that once children understand whether they are boys or girls, they actively watch for what their culture says boys and girls should be like, and then try to match those expectations. Which statement correctly describes this gender-schema theory?

dw.The view that children imitate same-gend: That is the social learning explanation of gender-typing.

bank.q: What is humanism?
bank.a: The view that people are capable of free choice, self-fulfillment and ethical behavior
d: The view that people are completely free and responsible for their own behavior
The view that personality is shaped by reinforcement
The view that personality reflects unconscious conflict
bank.why: Humanism is the “third force,” against the psychodynamic and behavioral models.
dh: The view that people are completely free and responsible for their own behavior
The view that people are capable of free choice but not of ethical behavior
The view that people are shaped toward self-fulfillment by reinforcement
bank.xq: One perspective on personality rejects the idea that people are driven only by unconscious urges or shaped only by rewards, and instead holds that people can choose freely, grow toward their full potential, and act morally. Which statement correctly describes humanism?

dw.The view that people are completely free: That is existentialism, which stresses complete freedom and responsibility.

bank.q: What is existentialism?
bank.a: The view that people are completely free and responsible for their own behavior
d: The view that people are capable of free choice, self-fulfillment and ethical behavior
The view that people define themselves by their groups
The view that personality is fixed in childhood
bank.why: It grew partly from the horrors of 20th-century war and genocide.
dh: The view that people are capable of free choice, self-fulfillment and ethical behavior
The view that people are completely free but not responsible for their own behavior
The view that people are partly free and their environment is responsible for their behavior
bank.xq: One philosophical view holds that human beings have no fixed nature handed to them, so each person is entirely free to choose and must therefore take full responsibility for whatever he or she does. Which statement correctly describes existentialism?

dw.The view that people are capable of free: That is humanism, which adds self-fulfillment and ethics.
dw.The view that people define themselves b: That is collectivism, a cultural idea.

bank.q: Viktor Frankl, Ludwig Binswanger and Medard Boss argued that
bank.a: seeing life as meaningless breeds apathy, so people must give life meaning
d: human life is trivial and meaningless in the grand scheme of things
personality is plastic and shaped mainly by the environment
traits are inherited and carried in the four bodily humors
bank.why: Sartre and Heidegger saw life as trivial; the psychiatrists said psychological salvation requires personal meaning and choices.
dh: seeing life as meaningful breeds apathy, so people must accept that life is meaningless
seeing life as meaningless breeds anxiety, so people must avoid thinking about meaning
life has a meaning given by society, so people must simply accept it
bank.xq: Some existentialist thinkers worked with people who felt their lives were empty and pointless, and who had lost the energy to care or act. What did Viktor Frankl, Ludwig Binswanger and Medard Boss argue about this?

dw.human life is trivial and meaningless in: That is Sartre's and Heidegger's view; the psychiatrists said life must be given meaning.

bank.q: In humanistic theory, what is self-actualization?
bank.a: The innate tendency to strive to realize one's potential
d: The mental image of the person we are capable of becoming
The automatic ejection of anxiety-evoking ideas
Beliefs that we can accomplish certain things
bank.why: Maslow saw it as a conscious, growth-oriented need; it requires taking risks.
dh: The learned tendency to strive to realize one's potential
The innate tendency to strive to meet others' conditions of worth
The mental image of the potential one could realize
bank.xq: Maslow and Rogers believed that a seed has within it the drive to grow into a full tree, and that people similarly have within them a drive to become all they can be. In humanistic theory, which statement describes this self-actualization?

bank.q: How did Carl Rogers define the self?
bank.a: The center of experience; your sense of who and what you are
d: The structure that uses reason to satisfy the id's demands without social disapproval
The mental image of the person you could become
A store of primitive images shared by the whole species
bank.why: Rogers said people shape themselves through free choice and action.
dh: The center of experience; your sense of who you could become
The center of the unconscious; your hidden sense of who you are
Your evaluation of whether you have value or merit
bank.xq: Carl Rogers made the self the center of his theory of personality. When a person asks, "Who am I, really?", Rogers would say the answer lies in the self. How did Rogers define the self?

bank.q: In Rogers's theory, what is the self-concept?
bank.a: Our impressions of ourselves and our evaluations of our own adequacy
d: The mental image of the person we are capable of becoming
Valuing a person regardless of how the person is behaving at the moment
The standards used to judge whether a person has value or merit
bank.why: Rogers was concerned with the self-concept and self-esteem.
dh: Others' impressions of us and their evaluations of our adequacy
Our impressions of the person we are capable of becoming
Our impressions of ourselves without any evaluation of our adequacy
bank.xq: A student thinks of herself as "kind, a bit shy, and not very good at math," and judges whether she is good enough as a person. In Rogers's theory, what term describes these impressions and evaluations?

bank.q: What are frames of reference in Rogers's theory?
bank.a: The unique ways each of us looks at ourselves and the world
d: Our impressions of ourselves and our evaluations of our own adequacy
The standards used to judge whether a person has value or merit
A firm sense of who one is and what one stands for
bank.why: One person judges the self by achievement–failure, another by decency–indecency.
dh: The shared ways a culture looks at itself and the world
The unique ways others look at us
The standards each of us uses to judge others' worth
bank.xq: Two students attend the same lecture. One sees the professor as inspiring, while the other sees him as boring and unfair, because each looks at the world through a lens shaped by his or her own experiences. In Rogers's theory, what are these lenses called?

bank.q: What is unconditional positive regard?
bank.a: Valuing a person regardless of how the person is behaving at the moment
d: Valuing a person only when the person behaves in an acceptable way
The standards used to judge whether a person has value or merit
The mental image of the person we are capable of becoming
bank.why: It is not approval of every behavior. Parents who show it help children develop self-esteem.
dh: Valuing a person only when the person is behaving well at the moment
Valuing a person's behavior regardless of who the person is
Approving of everything a person does at the moment
bank.xq: A mother scolds her son for breaking a window but still makes it clear that she loves and values him as a person no matter what he has done. In Rogers's theory, which statement correctly describes the kind of regard she shows?

bank.q: What is conditional positive regard?
bank.a: Valuing a person only when the person behaves in an acceptable way
d: Valuing a person regardless of how the person is behaving at the moment
The standards used to judge whether a person has value or merit
Our impressions of ourselves and our evaluations of our own adequacy
bank.why: Children valued only when they behave as wished may develop conditions of worth.
dh: Valuing a person regardless of how the person behaves
Valuing a person's acceptable behavior regardless of who the person is
Valuing a person only when the person reaches their own self-ideal
bank.xq: A child senses that her parents show her love and approval only when she is quiet, obedient and gets good grades, and withdraw it when she misbehaves. Which statement correctly describes this kind of regard?

bank.q: What are conditions of worth?
bank.a: The standards used to judge whether a person has value or merit
d: Valuing a person regardless of how the person is behaving at the moment
Valuing a person only when the person behaves in an acceptable way
The mental image of the person we are capable of becoming
bank.why: Children may come to think they have merit only if they meet these standards.
dh: The standards used to judge whether a behavior is acceptable to society
The standards a person uses to judge their own potential
The value given to a person regardless of their behavior
bank.xq: A child learns that he is worth loving only if he wins competitions and keeps a clean room. Rogers said that such standards, which the child absorbs from others, can distort his self-concept. Which statement correctly describes these conditions of worth?

dw.Valuing a person only when the person be: That is conditional positive regard, which can create conditions of worth.

bank.q: In Rogers's theory, what is the self-ideal?
bank.a: The mental image of the person we are capable of becoming
d: Our impressions of ourselves and our evaluations of our own adequacy
Valuing a person regardless of how the person is behaving at the moment
Our ongoing sense of who and what we are
bank.why: We are motivated to reduce the gap between self-concept and self-ideal; the closer they are, the healthier we are.
dh: The mental image of the person we are right now
The mental image of the person others want us to be
The innate drive to become the person we are capable of being
bank.xq: A nursing student pictures herself years from now as a calm, skilled and compassionate nurse, someone she believes she has it in her to become. In Rogers's theory, which statement correctly describes this self-ideal?

dw.Our ongoing sense of who and what we are: That is the self, the center of experience.

bank.q: A father praises his son only when he gets perfect grades and is cold otherwise. Rogers would call this
bank.a: conditional positive regard
d: unconditional positive regard
congruence
self-actualization
bank.why: Acceptance depends on behavior, which can create conditions of worth.
bank.xq: A father warmly praises and hugs his son only when he brings home perfect grades, and treats him coldly whenever he falls short. Over time the boy feels he is worth loving only when he performs. Rogers would call the father's attitude

dw.unconditional positive regard: His acceptance depends on grades, so it is conditional.
dw.congruence: Congruence is a fit between self-concept and experience, not a way of valuing someone.
dw.self-actualization: Self-actualization is striving to realize one's potential, not a parenting pattern.

bank.q: According to Rogers, anxiety often stems from
bank.a: feelings and desires that clash with a distorted self-concept
d: unresolved Oedipus or Electra conflicts from childhood
an imbalance of the bodily humors, such as black bile
too little reinforcement for the behaviors one wants
bank.why: To keep their self-concept, people may deny their genuine feelings.
dh: feelings and desires that fit an accurate self-concept
feelings and desires that clash with the superego's standards
a distorted self-concept that matches one's self-ideal
bank.xq: A young man was taught that boys should never feel afraid, so he sees himself as fearless. When he feels fear before an exam, he becomes anxious because the feeling does not fit the way he sees himself. According to Rogers, where does anxiety like this often come from?

bank.q: What is both the main strength and the main weakness of the humanistic–existential approach?
bank.a: Its focus on private, subjective conscious experience
d: Its reliance on case studies of the unconscious mind and early childhood
Its use of factor analysis to find basic traits
Its claim that personality is plastic and learned
bank.why: It also says little about how traits and personality types develop.
dh: Its focus on public, observable behavior
Its focus on private, unconscious experience
Its focus on inherited, measurable traits
bank.xq: The humanistic–existential approach is praised for valuing people's own experience of themselves, but it is also criticized because such experience cannot be directly observed or easily tested. What is both the main strength and the main weakness of this approach?

dw.Its use of factor analysis to find basic: That is how trait theorists work.

bank.q: What is the sociocultural perspective on personality?
bank.a: The view that ethnicity, gender and culture shape personality
d: The view that personality is shaped by unconscious conflicts from childhood
The view that personality is five inherited factors
The view that personality is shaped by reinforcement alone
bank.why: It explains why behavior that seems normal in one culture seems brazen in another.
dh: The view that ethnicity, gender and culture are shaped by personality
The view that genes and hormones shape personality
The view that ethnicity, gender and culture have little effect on personality
bank.xq: A psychologist explains a student's personality by looking at her ethnic background, the gender roles she grew up with, and the values of the culture she belongs to. Which statement correctly describes this sociocultural perspective on personality?

bank.q: What is an individualist?
bank.a: A person who defines the self by personal traits and puts personal goals first
d: A person who defines the self by groups and relationships and puts group goals first
A person who keeps the customs of the old country only
A person who blends the customs of two cultures
bank.why: People in the United States and northern Europe tend to be individualistic.
dh: A person who defines the self by personal traits but puts group goals first
A person who defines the self by groups but puts personal goals first
A person who defines the self by groups and puts group goals first
bank.xq: Some people describe themselves mainly in terms of their own traits and abilities, and when their own goals conflict with what their group wants, they tend to put their own goals first. Which statement correctly describes such an individualist?

dw.A person who keeps the customs of the ol: That describes someone who keeps only the old culture (separated).

bank.q: What is a collectivist?
bank.a: A person who defines the self by groups and relationships and puts group goals first
d: A person who defines the self by personal traits and puts personal goals first
A person who fully adopts the new dominant culture and drops the old
A person who keeps the old culture and avoids the new one
bank.why: Many people in Africa, Asia and Central and South America tend to be collectivistic.
dh: A person who defines the self by groups and relationships but puts personal goals first
A person who defines the self by personal traits but puts group goals first
A person who defines the self by personal traits and puts personal goals first
bank.xq: Some people describe themselves mainly in terms of the groups they belong to and their relationships with others, and when their own wishes conflict with those of their family or group, they put the group first. Which statement correctly describes such a collectivist?

bank.q: Asked to complete “I am …,” Ken answers “I am a father, I am a Buddhist, I am Japanese.” His answers suggest he is
bank.a: a collectivist
d: an individualist
bicultural
assimilated
bank.why: Collectivists describe themselves by family, religion and nation; individualists by traits and jobs.
bank.xq: In a study, participants are asked to complete the sentence "I am …" in several ways. Ken writes: "I am a father," "I am a Buddhist," and "I am Japanese," describing himself through his roles and groups rather than his personal traits. His answers suggest that he is

dw.an individualist: Individualists describe themselves by traits and jobs, not by family and nation.
dw.bicultural: Bicultural describes mixing two cultures, not how someone defines the self.
dw.assimilated: Assimilated means fully adopting a new culture, not defining the self by groups.

bank.q: What is acculturation?
bank.a: Adapting to a new dominant culture by learning its ways
d: Keeping the language and customs of the country of origin only
Defining oneself by the goals of one's group
Developing traits that fit stereotypical gender roles
bank.why: Immigrants may become assimilated, separated or bicultural.
dh: Adapting a new culture to fit one's own ways
Refusing a new dominant culture and keeping one's own ways
Passing one's own culture's ways on to one's children
bank.xq: A student from the province moves to a big city for college and gradually learns the city's way of speaking, dressing and doing things in order to fit in. Which statement correctly describes this process of acculturation?

dw.Keeping the language and customs of the: That is separation: keeping only the old culture.

bank.q: An immigrant speaks her native language at home, English at work, and switches between both cultures' values as needed. She is
bank.a: bicultural
d: assimilated
separated
individualistic
bank.why: Bicultural people blend both cultures and can switch “mental gears.”
bank.xq: An immigrant nurse speaks her native language with her family at home, speaks English at the hospital, and switches between the values of both cultures depending on where she is, without giving up either one. Which term best describes her?

dw.assimilated: Assimilated people drop their native culture.
dw.separated: Separated people keep only their native culture.
dw.individualistic: Individualistic describes how the self is defined, not mixing two cultures.

bank.q: An immigrant drops his native language and customs and identifies fully with the new country's culture. He is
bank.a: assimilated
d: bicultural
separated
collectivistic
bank.why: Assimilation means fully adopting the dominant culture.
bank.xq: After moving abroad, an immigrant stops speaking his native language, drops the customs he grew up with, and now identifies fully with his new country's culture. Which term best describes him?

dw.separated: Separated people keep only the old culture.
dw.collectivistic: Collectivistic describes a group-centered self, not dropping a culture.

bank.q: Which immigrants tend to have the highest self-esteem?
bank.a: Those who keep their traditions while learning the new culture
d: Those who abandon their native language and customs completely
Those who avoid the new culture and keep only the old
Those who define themselves only by personal traits
bank.why: People who do not fully give up their backgrounds have higher self-esteem; English proficiency also lowers anxiety and depression.
dh: Those who drop their traditions while learning the new culture
Those who keep their traditions and avoid the new culture
Those who drop their traditions and avoid the new culture
bank.xq: Research compared immigrants who handled their move to a new culture in different ways, for example by holding onto or dropping their old traditions and by learning or avoiding the new culture's ways. Which immigrants tend to have the highest self-esteem?

dw.Those who abandon their native language: Fully giving up their background goes with lower self-esteem.
dw.Those who avoid the new culture and keep: Avoiding the new culture is separation, which does not give the highest self-esteem.
dw.Those who define themselves only by pers: Defining the self only by traits is individualism, not a way of adapting to a new culture.

bank.q: In psychological testing, what is validity?
bank.a: The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure
d: The consistency of test scores from one testing to another
Comparing a person's score with scores of people of the same age and group
Checking each occurrence of a behavior within a time frame
bank.why: Validity is usually checked against external criteria, like teachers' reports of hyperactivity.
dh: The degree to which a test gives the same scores from one testing to another
The degree to which a test compares a person with others of the same age
The degree to which a test measures what the test-taker wants it to measure
bank.xq: A test claims to measure anxiety, but its items actually reflect how good a person is at reading. A psychologist says the test lacks an important quality. In psychological testing, which statement describes this quality, called validity?

bank.q: In psychological testing, what is reliability?
bank.a: The consistency of test scores from one testing to another
d: The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure
Comparing a person's score with scores of people of the same age and group
Answering items in a specified, limited manner
bank.why: A reliable IQ test gives similar scores in childhood, adolescence and adulthood.
dh: The accuracy of a test in measuring what it is supposed to measure
The consistency of a person's behavior from one situation to another
The consistency of a person's score with scores of others of the same age
bank.xq: A student takes the same personality test twice, two weeks apart, and gets very different scores even though nothing about her has changed. A psychologist says the test lacks an important quality. Which statement describes this quality, called reliability?

bank.q: What is test standardization?
bank.a: Comparing a person's score with scores of people of the same age and group
d: The degree to which a test measures what it is supposed to measure, as shown by research
The consistency of test scores from one testing to another
Presenting ambiguous stimuli onto which people project their personality
bank.why: We cannot judge one person's score without comparing it with people of the same age and group.
dh: Comparing a person's score with their own earlier score on the test
Comparing a person's score with scores of people of all ages and groups
Checking whether a test measures what it is supposed to measure
bank.xq: A 20-year-old's score on a personality test is interpreted by comparing it with the scores of a large group of other 20-year-old students who took the same test. What is this process of test standardization?

bank.q: What is a behavior-rating scale?
bank.a: Trained observers checking off each occurrence of a behavior
d: A questionnaire whose items have specific correct answers scored by an answer key
A test of ambiguous inkblots that people describe
A test in which people tell stories about pictures
bank.why: Used in settings such as classrooms or mental hospitals.
dh: Untrained observers rating a person's overall personality
People checking off how often they think they show a behavior
Trained observers telling stories about a person's behavior
bank.xq: In a school study, trained observers sit in a classroom and put a check mark on a form every time a particular child hits another child or leaves his seat. What kind of assessment is this?

dw.A test of ambiguous inkblots that people: That is the Rorschach, a projective test.
dw.A test in which people tell stories abou: That is the TAT, a projective test.

bank.q: What is an objective test?
bank.a: A test whose items must be answered in a specified, limited manner
d: A test that presents ambiguous stimuli and allows a broad range of answers
Trained observers recording behavior in a setting
A test that measures what it is supposed to measure
bank.why: Example: true–false or forced-choice items.
dh: A test whose items may be answered in any manner the person likes
A test whose items are scored by the examiner's impressions
A test whose items are ambiguous pictures answered freely
bank.xq: A personality test asks people to answer each item only "true" or "false," or to choose one of a few given options, with no room for free answers. Which statement correctly describes such an objective test?

bank.q: What is a projective test?
bank.a: A test with ambiguous stimuli onto which people project their personality
d: A test whose items must be answered in a specified, limited manner
A true–false questionnaire built from clinical interview data
Trained observers recording each behavior in a classroom setting
bank.why: Examples: Rorschach inkblots and the TAT.
dh: A test with clear stimuli onto which people project their personality
A test with ambiguous stimuli answered in a specified, limited manner
A test in which examiners project their own personality onto the client
bank.xq: A client is shown an inkblot that has no clear shape and asked what it might be. The psychologist assumes that whatever the client sees reveals something about her own needs and feelings. Which statement correctly describes this kind of projective test?

dw.A true–false questionnaire built from cl: That describes an objective test like the MMPI.

bank.q: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is
bank.a: an objective true–false test used to help diagnose disorders
d: a projective test made up of ambiguous inkblots
a test in which people make up stories about pictures
a behavior-rating scale used in classrooms
bank.why: It is the most widely used test in clinical work; its scales were built empirically from clinical data.
dh: a projective true–false test used to help diagnose disorders
an objective multiple-choice test used to measure the Big Five
an objective true–false test used to measure intelligence
bank.xq: The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) is one of the most widely used personality tests in clinical settings. Which statement correctly describes the MMPI?

bank.q: How were the MMPI scales constructed?
bank.a: Empirically, keeping items that set apart people with symptoms
d: From Freud's theory of the three psychic structures
From the five broad factors of the Big Five model
From stories people told about ambiguous pictures
bank.why: Items came from questions often asked in clinical interviews.
dh: Theoretically, keeping items that fit Freud's three psychic structures
Empirically, keeping items that all people answered the same way
Rationally, keeping items experts thought sounded like symptoms
bank.xq: The MMPI's scales were not built by asking experts which questions sounded like symptoms of a disorder. Instead, test makers compared how different groups of people actually answered the items. How were the MMPI scales constructed?

dw.From Freud's theory of the three psychic: The MMPI scales did not come from Freud's theory.
dw.From the five broad factors of the Big F: The Big Five led to the NEO inventory, not the MMPI.
dw.From stories people told about ambiguous: Stories about pictures are the TAT.

bank.q: “I would rather (a) be a forest ranger, (b) work in a busy office, (c) play a musical instrument.” This item is typical of
bank.a: an interest inventory (forced choice)
d: a projective personality test with ambiguous items
the Rorschach Inkblot Test of personality
a behavior-rating scale filled out by an observer
bank.why: Interest inventories help predict whether a person would do well in an occupation.
bank.xq: A career guidance test asks, "I would rather (a) be a forest ranger, (b) work in a busy office, or (c) play a musical instrument," and the student must pick one even if she likes none of them. An item like this is typical of

dw.a projective personality test with ambig: The choices are fixed (forced choice), so it is not projective.
dw.a behavior-rating scale filled out by an: A behavior-rating scale is filled out by an observer, not the person.

bank.q: Who created the best-known inkblot test?
bank.a: Hermann Rorschach
d: Henry Murray of Harvard
Hans Eysenck
Gordon Allport
bank.why: Test-takers say what each blot looks like or could be.
bank.xq: One of the best-known projective tests asks people to say what they see in a series of symmetrical inkblots, some in color and some in black and white. Who created this best-known inkblot test?

bank.q: On the Rorschach, a response that accurately reflects the shape of the blot is a sign of
bank.a: adequate reality testing
d: neuroticism
high intellectual functioning
collectivism
bank.why: A response that richly combines several features of the blot suggests high intellectual functioning.
bank.xq: When taking the Rorschach, one client describes shapes that really match the outline of the inkblot, while another describes things that do not fit the blot's shape at all. A response that accurately reflects the shape of the blot is a sign of

dw.neuroticism: Accurate shapes show reality testing, not neuroticism.
dw.high intellectual functioning: High intellectual functioning shows in responses that richly combine several features.
dw.collectivism: Collectivism is a cultural self-definition, not a Rorschach score.

bank.q: Who developed the Thematic Apperception Test, in which people make up stories about ambiguous drawings?
bank.a: Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan
d: Hermann Rorschach
Robert McCrae and Paul Costa
David McClelland
bank.why: It is widely used for motivation research and to assess needs and relationships.
bank.xq: In one projective test, people look at ambiguous drawings and are asked to make up a story about each one: what is happening, what led up to it and how it will end. Who developed this Thematic Apperception Test?

dw.Robert McCrae and Paul Costa: McCrae and Costa built the NEO inventory.
dw.David McClelland: McClelland used the TAT in research but did not develop it.

bank.q: A client looks at a drawing of a woman by a window and is asked what led up to the scene and what will happen next. This is the
bank.a: Thematic Apperception Test
d: Rorschach Inkblot Test
Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory
NEO Five-Factor Inventory
bank.why: People are assumed to project their own needs into the stories.
bank.xq: A client is shown a vague drawing of a woman standing by a window. The psychologist asks her what the woman is thinking, what led up to this moment, and what will happen next, and then studies the themes in her story. Which test is being given?

dw.Rorschach Inkblot Test: The Rorschach uses inkblots, not drawings and stories.
dw.Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Invent: The MMPI is a true-false questionnaire.
dw.NEO Five-Factor Inventory: The NEO is a questionnaire for the Big Five.

bank.q: Can psychologists determine for sure whether someone told the truth on a personality test?
bank.a: No; there can be signs of deception, but no guarantees
d: Yes, because the MMPI always reveals who is lying
Yes, because projective tests cannot be faked or consciously controlled
No, because personality tests never check for lying
bank.why: From the book's “truth or fiction” items.
dh: Yes; validity scales guarantee who is lying
No; tests have no way to detect possible deception
Yes; projective tests cannot be faked, so they always reveal lies
bank.xq: A job applicant wants to look as good as possible, so she answers a personality test in the way she thinks the employer wants. Some tests include scales that flag answers that seem too good to be true. Can psychologists determine for sure whether someone told the truth on a personality test?

dw.Yes, because the MMPI always reveals who: The MMPI has lie checks, but they cannot guarantee anything.
dw.Yes, because projective tests cannot be: Projective tests can also be faked.
dw.No, because personality tests never chec: Some tests do include checks for lying; they are just not perfect.

bank.q: How do psychologists define stress?
bank.a: The demand made on an organism to adapt, cope or adjust
d: Healthful stress that keeps us alert and motivated
Stress perceived as threatening or overwhelming that harms health
A pressure or force exerted on a physical body
bank.why: In physics stress is a force on a body; in psychology it is the demand to adapt.
dh: The response of an organism after it fails to adapt, cope or adjust
The demand an organism makes on its environment to change
Only harmful demands that an organism cannot cope with
bank.xq: A student has an exam tomorrow, a part-time job, and a sick parent at home. Each of these places a demand on her that she must deal with in some way. How do psychologists define stress?

dw.A pressure or force exerted on a physica: That is stress in physics, not psychology.

bank.q: What is eustress?
bank.a: Healthful stress that keeps us alert and motivated
d: Stress perceived as threatening or overwhelming that harms health
The demand made on an organism to adapt, cope or adjust
A microscopic organism that can cause disease
bank.why: Hans Selye's term. Starting a sought-after job can be eustress.
dh: Harmful stress that keeps us alert but drains us
Healthful stress that keeps us calm and relaxed
The absence of stress, which keeps us motivated
bank.xq: A runner feels a rush of nervous energy before a race that makes her more focused and pushes her to perform her best. Not all stress is harmful, and this kind is actually good for us. Which statement correctly describes eustress?

dw.The demand made on an organism to adapt,: That is the general definition of stress.

bank.q: Who called healthful stress eustress?
bank.a: Hans Selye
d: Albert Ellis
Richard Lazarus
Walter Cannon
bank.why: Selye (1907–1982) was the stress researcher behind the general adaptation syndrome.
bank.xq: One researcher pointed out that some stress is actually healthy because it keeps us alert and motivated, and he coined a special term for this healthful stress, eustress. Who called healthful stress eustress?

dw.Richard Lazarus: Richard Lazarus studied hassles and appraisal.
dw.Walter Cannon: Walter Cannon described fight or flight.

bank.q: What is health psychology?
bank.a: The study of how psychological factors affect physical illness and its treatment
d: The study of relationships among psychology, the nervous system and the immune system
The study of how to classify and diagnose psychological disorders
The study of personality traits and how to measure them
bank.why: Health psychologists study stress, coping, seeking care and health education.
dh: The study of how physical illness affects psychological disorders and their treatment
The study of how psychological factors, the nervous system and immunity interact
The study of how to prevent psychological disorders through healthy habits
