bank.xq: A psychologist studies how stress, attitudes and habits such as smoking or exercise influence whether people develop heart disease, and how patients cope with treatment. What field of psychology is this?

dw.The study of how to classify and diagnos: That is classifying and diagnosing disorders.

bank.q: What is a pathogen?
bank.a: A microscopic organism, such as a virus, that can cause disease
d: A substance that stimulates the body to mount an immune response
A white blood cell that engulfs foreign agents
A protein that recognizes and destroys antigens
bank.why: Stress and pathogens interact to influence the immune system.
dh: A microscopic organism, such as a white blood cell, that fights disease
A substance, such as a weakened virus, that triggers immunity but cannot cause disease
A protein, such as an antibody, that can cause disease
bank.xq: Viruses, bacteria and other tiny organisms can enter the body and make a person sick. In health psychology, which statement correctly describes such a pathogen?

bank.q: What are daily hassles?
bank.a: Regular experiences that threaten or harm our well-being
d: Positive or negative events that occur at irregular intervals
Feelings of being pulled in two directions by opposing motives
Beliefs that blow negative events out of proportion
bank.why: Richard Lazarus and colleagues listed eight kinds.
dh: Irregular experiences that threaten or harm our well-being
Regular experiences that improve our well-being
Irregular positive or negative events that require adjustment
bank.xq: A commuter deals with traffic jams every morning, misplaces things, and worries about bills, small problems that come up again and again and slowly wear her down. Which statement best describes these daily hassles?

bank.q: A nursing student has three requirements due tomorrow and not enough hours to finish. This is which kind of hassle?
bank.a: Time-pressure
d: Inner concern
Household
Security
bank.why: Too many things to do and not enough time.
bank.xq: It is 9 p.m., and a nursing student realizes she has three requirements due tomorrow morning and not nearly enough hours to finish them all. Which kind of hassle is she experiencing?

dw.Inner concern: Inner concern hassles are things like loneliness or isolation.
dw.Household: Household hassles are chores and home upkeep.
dw.Security: Security hassles are about job, investments and safety.

bank.q: A transferee feels socially isolated and lonely in her new school. This is which kind of hassle?
bank.a: Inner concern
d: Environmental
Work
Health
bank.why: Inner concern hassles: being socially isolated, lonely.
bank.xq: A transferee has trouble making friends in her new school. She often eats alone and feels socially isolated and lonely, even though everything else in her life is going well. Which kind of hassle is this?

dw.Environmental: Environmental hassles are noise, crime and pollution.
dw.Work: Work hassles are about the job or its duties.

bank.q: Constant traffic noise, pollution and crime near your boarding house are
bank.a: environmental hassles
d: security hassles
household hassles
financial responsibility hassles
bank.why: Environmental: crime, weather, noise, pollution.
bank.xq: A student's boarding house is beside a busy highway. The constant traffic noise keeps her up at night, the air is polluted, and she has heard of several crimes in the area. What kind of hassles are these?

dw.security hassles: Security hassles are about job and money safety.
dw.household hassles: Household hassles are chores and repairs.
dw.financial responsibility hassles: Financial responsibility hassles are about bills and debts.

bank.q: Worrying about keeping a job, investments and retirement are
bank.a: security hassles
d: work hassles
financial responsibility hassles
time-pressure hassles
bank.why: Security: job security, terrorism, investments, retirement.
bank.xq: A 40-year-old worries that his company may close, that his investments may lose value, and that he will not have enough money when he retires. What kind of hassles are these?

dw.work hassles: Work hassles are about duties and the job itself, not security.
dw.financial responsibility hassles: Financial responsibility hassles are about bills and debts.
dw.time-pressure hassles: Time-pressure hassles are too much to do and too little time.

bank.q: How do life changes differ from daily hassles?
bank.a: Life changes can be positive and are irregular; hassles are negative and regular
d: Life changes are always negative, while daily hassles can be positive
Life changes happen every day, while hassles happen only once
There is no real difference; both are always negative
bank.why: Both require adjustment, which is why even good changes are stressful.
bank.hint: Good or bad, now and then.
dh: Life changes are negative and irregular; hassles can be positive and are regular
Life changes can be positive and are regular; hassles are negative and irregular
Life changes are always negative and regular; hassles are positive and irregular
bank.xq: Getting married, moving to a new city and starting college all require adjustment, just like losing your keys and sitting in traffic. Yet psychologists distinguish the first group from the second. How do life changes differ from daily hassles?

dw.Life changes are always negative, while: Reversed: life changes can be positive, and hassles are the negative daily ones.
dw.Life changes happen every day, while has: Reversed: hassles are regular, and life changes are irregular.
dw.There is no real difference; both are al: They do differ: life changes can be positive and are irregular.

bank.q: Why can positive events like graduating or going on vacation be stressful?
bank.a: They are life changes, and changes require adjustment
d: They raise the number of daily hassles to dangerous levels
They always cause approach–avoidance conflict
They always involve catastrophizing
bank.why: On the life-change scale, academic success scored 54 units and vacation 30.
dh: They are daily hassles, and hassles require adjustment
They are life changes, and changes are always negative
They cause approach–avoidance conflict, which requires adjustment
bank.xq: A student is excited to graduate and go on a long vacation, yet she finds herself tense and having trouble sleeping. Her friend is surprised, since these are happy events. Why can positive events like graduating or going on vacation be stressful?

dw.They raise the number of daily hassles t: Positive events are not hassles; they are life changes.
dw.They always cause approach–avoidance con: They do not always cause conflict.
dw.They always involve catastrophizing: They do not always involve catastrophizing.

bank.q: On the college students' life-change scale, which event was rated the most stressful?
bank.a: Death of a spouse
d: Beginning college
Academic failure
Graduating from college
bank.why: Death of a spouse = 94 units; beginning college 84; academic failure 77; graduating 68.
bank.xq: Researchers developed a scale to measure how stressful various life changes are for college students, rating events such as beginning college, academic failure and graduating. On this college students' life-change scale, which event was rated the most stressful?

dw.Beginning college: Beginning college scored 84, below the death of a spouse at 94.

bank.q: According to the Stress in America surveys, which are the two most common stressors?
bank.a: Money and work
d: Health and weather
School and traffic
Relationships and social media
bank.why: Money 62%, work 61%; listening to music (47%) and exercise (46%) are top coping methods.
bank.xq: Every year, the Stress in America surveys ask adults what causes them the most stress in their lives, such as health, relationships, the economy and the news. According to these surveys, which are the two most common stressors?

dw.Health and weather: Money and work lead; health and weather are not the top two.
dw.School and traffic: School and traffic are not the top two.
dw.Relationships and social media: Relationships and social media are not the top two.

bank.q: In psychology, what is conflict?
bank.a: Being pulled in two or more directions by opposing motives
d: Interpreting negative events as total disasters
A regularly occurring experience that harms well-being or threatens it
Hostility and competitiveness shown toward other people
bank.why: Conflict is stressful; there are four types.
dh: Being pulled in one direction by two matching motives
Being pushed by others in a direction one does not want to go
Blowing a choice between opposing motives out of proportion
bank.xq: A student wants to go to a party with friends but also wants to study for an important exam, and feels torn between the two. In psychology, which statement correctly describes this state of conflict?

dw.Hostility and competitiveness shown towa: That describes the hostility and competitiveness of Type A behavior.

bank.q: What is an approach–approach conflict?
bank.a: A choice between two desirable goals that are both within reach
d: A choice between two undesirable outcomes, both hard to avoid or delay
A single goal that has both positive and negative sides
Several options, each with its own pluses and minuses
bank.why: The least stressful type (Neal Miller); usually resolved by making a decision.
dh: A choice between two desirable goals, only one of which is within reach
A choice between two undesirable outcomes that are both within reach
A single desirable goal that is within reach but has a cost
bank.xq: A graduating student is accepted into two nursing schools she likes equally, and either one is hers if she enrolls. She feels stressed only because she has to give up one to take the other. Which statement correctly describes this kind of conflict?

bank.q: What is an avoidance–avoidance conflict?
bank.a: A choice between two undesirable outcomes, both hard to avoid
d: A choice between two desirable goals that are both within reach
A single goal that has both positive and negative sides
Several options, each with its own pluses and minuses
bank.why: Some people withdraw or do nothing when no resolution is in sight.
dh: A choice between two undesirable outcomes, both easy to avoid
A choice between two desirable goals, both hard to reach
A single undesirable outcome that has a hidden benefit
bank.xq: A student must choose between doing a long, boring project she dreads and taking a failing grade she also dreads, and there is no way to escape both. Which statement correctly describes this kind of conflict?

bank.q: What is an approach–avoidance conflict?
bank.a: A single goal that has both positive and negative sides
d: A choice between two desirable goals that are both within reach
A choice between two undesirable outcomes, both hard to avoid
Several options, each with its own pluses and minuses
bank.why: Such goals look attractive from a distance and less so up close.
dh: Two goals, one positive and one negative, to choose between
A single goal that has only negative sides
Several goals, each with both positive and negative sides
bank.xq: A student wants to join the varsity team because it would be fun and good for her résumé, but joining also means long practices and less time to study. Which statement correctly describes this kind of conflict?

bank.q: Choosing between pizza and tacos, both of which you love, is an example of
bank.a: approach–approach conflict
d: avoidance–avoidance conflict
approach–avoidance conflict
multiple approach–avoidance conflict
bank.why: Two desirable goals; the least stressful type.
bank.xq: Hungry after class, you are trying to decide whether to order pizza or tacos. You love both equally, and either one is easily available. What type of conflict is this?

dw.avoidance–avoidance conflict: Avoidance-avoidance means both choices are unpleasant.
dw.approach–avoidance conflict: Approach-avoidance is one goal with good and bad sides.
dw.multiple approach–avoidance conflict: Multiple approach-avoidance compares options that each have pluses and minuses.

bank.q: You fear the dentist but also fear your teeth will decay if you don't go. This is
bank.a: avoidance–avoidance conflict
d: approach–avoidance conflict
approach–approach conflict
multiple approach–avoidance conflict
bank.why: Both outcomes are undesirable.
bank.xq: You are afraid of going to the dentist because of the pain, but you are also afraid that your teeth will decay if you keep putting it off, and you cannot escape both. What type of conflict is this?

dw.approach–avoidance conflict: Approach-avoidance is one goal with good and bad sides.
dw.approach–approach conflict: Approach-approach means both choices are desirable.
dw.multiple approach–avoidance conflict: Multiple approach-avoidance compares several options, each with pluses and minuses.

bank.q: Cheesecake is delicious, but oh, the calories. This is
bank.a: approach–avoidance conflict
d: avoidance–avoidance conflict
approach–approach conflict
multiple approach–avoidance conflict
bank.why: One goal with good and bad points.
bank.xq: At a party, you see a slice of cheesecake. It looks delicious and you really want it, but you also know it is full of calories, so the same dessert both attracts and repels you. What type of conflict is this?

dw.avoidance–avoidance conflict: Avoidance-avoidance means both choices are unpleasant.
dw.approach–approach conflict: Approach-approach means both choices are desirable.
dw.multiple approach–avoidance conflict: Multiple approach-avoidance compares several options, each with pluses and minuses.

bank.q: The night before an exam you must choose between studying (boring, but no worry) and a movie (fun, but you'll worry). This is
bank.a: multiple approach–avoidance conflict
d: approach–approach conflict
avoidance–avoidance conflict
approach–avoidance conflict
bank.why: Several alternatives, each with pluses and minuses; the most complex type.
bank.xq: The night before an exam, you must choose between studying, which is boring but means you will not worry, and going to a movie, which is fun but means you will worry about the exam. Each option has both good and bad sides. What type of conflict is this?

dw.approach–approach conflict: Approach-approach means both choices are desirable.
dw.avoidance–avoidance conflict: Avoidance-avoidance means both choices are unpleasant.
dw.approach–avoidance conflict: Approach-avoidance is one goal with good and bad sides; here two options each have both.

bank.q: In Albert Ellis's A → B → C approach, what does B stand for?
bank.a: Beliefs about the event
d: Behavior after the event
Bodily arousal
Blame placed on others
bank.why: A = activating event, B = beliefs, C = consequences. Beliefs, not just events, are stressors.
bank.xq: Albert Ellis argued that it is not an event itself that makes us feel bad, but something that comes between the event and our emotional reaction. In his A → B → C approach, A is the activating event and C is the consequence. What does B stand for?

dw.Bodily arousal: B is Beliefs, not bodily arousal.
dw.Blame placed on others: B is Beliefs; blaming others is only one possible belief.

bank.q: According to Ellis, a situation like failing a test, which results in stress, is called the
bank.a: activating event
d: stimulus event-response event
causal event
consequence
bank.why: Losing a job is an activating event (A); misery is the consequence (C).
bank.xq: Albert Ellis explained stress with an A → B → C model. A student fails a test, believes this means she is a total failure, and then feels depressed and anxious. In Ellis's terms, what is the failed test, the situation that starts this chain, called?

dw.stimulus event-response event: Ellis does not use the term stimulus event.
dw.causal event: Ellis does not call it a causal event; he says beliefs, not events, cause the stress.
dw.consequence: The consequence (C) is the misery that follows.

bank.q: What does it mean to catastrophize?
bank.a: To blow negative events out of proportion
d: To believe one can bring about desired changes oneself
To see change as a normal chance for personal growth
To blame one's failures on luck and outside forces
bank.why: Catastrophizing raises anxiety, depression and even blood pressure.
dh: To downplay negative events as if they did not matter
To blow positive events out of proportion
To blame negative events on outside forces
bank.xq: After getting one low quiz score, a student tells herself, "This is a disaster; I'll fail the whole course, lose my scholarship and ruin my future." Which statement correctly describes what she is doing when she catastrophizes?

dw.To see change as a normal chance for per: That is the challenge element of hardiness.
dw.To blame one's failures on luck and outs: That is an external locus of control.

bank.q: Edward's professor says his paper could have been shorter. Edward concludes he cannot write and will surely fail the class. This is
bank.a: catastrophizing
d: approach–avoidance conflict
psychological hardiness
an external locus of control
bank.why: He blows a minor event out of proportion.
bank.xq: Edward's professor returns his paper with the comment that it could have been shorter. Edward concludes that he simply cannot write, that the professor hates his work, and that he will surely fail the class. Which of the following best describes Edward's reaction?

dw.approach–avoidance conflict: Approach-avoidance is a conflict over one goal's good and bad sides.
dw.psychological hardiness: Hardiness would treat this as a challenge, not a disaster.
dw.an external locus of control: An external locus would blame luck or others; Edward exaggerates the event itself.

bank.q: Which is one of Ellis's irrational beliefs?
bank.a: One must have the approval of important people almost all the time
d: Change, rather than stability, is a normal part of life
I can bring about desired changes through my own efforts
Some stress is healthy because it keeps us alert and busy
bank.why: Others: we must be thoroughly competent; human misery is caused from outside; the past must affect us forever.
dh: It is nice, but not necessary, to have the approval of important people
One should seek the approval of important people only some of the time
Change, rather than stability, is a normal part of life
bank.xq: Albert Ellis listed a number of irrational beliefs that make people more vulnerable to stress, such as demanding perfection or insisting that life must always be fair. Which of the following is one of Ellis's irrational beliefs?

dw.Change, rather than stability, is a norm: That is a healthy belief, not one of Ellis's irrational beliefs.
dw.I can bring about desired changes throug: That is self-efficacy, a healthy belief.
dw.Some stress is healthy because it keeps: That is a healthy view of stress.

bank.q: What is the Type A behavior pattern?
bank.a: Behavior marked by time urgency, competitiveness, impatience and hostility
d: Behavior marked by relaxing readily and focusing on quality of life
Commitment, challenge and control that buffer stress
Interpreting minor negative events as total disasters
bank.why: Also called the coronary-prone behavior pattern.
dh: Behavior marked by time urgency, cooperation, patience and hostility
Behavior marked by relaxed pacing, competitiveness, impatience and hostility
Behavior marked by time urgency, competitiveness, patience and friendliness
bank.xq: A manager is always rushing, gets irritated when others are slow, turns every task into a contest, and quickly becomes angry with coworkers. Which statement correctly describes the behavior pattern he shows?

bank.q: Which behavior pattern is called coronary-prone?
bank.a: Type A
d: Type B
Psychological hardiness
Tend-and-befriend
bank.why: Type A people show higher blood pressure in response to stressors.
bank.xq: Researchers found that people who show a certain pattern of behavior, marked by time urgency, competitiveness and hostility, have a higher risk of heart disease. Which behavior pattern is described as coronary-prone?

dw.Type B: Type B people are relaxed, not coronary-prone.
dw.Tend-and-befriend: Tend-and-befriend is a stress response, not a pattern linked to heart disease.

bank.q: Which quotation best represents the Type A personality?
bank.a: “Winning isn't everything; it's the only thing.”
d: “Don't worry, be happy.”
“Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.”
“All for one and one for all.”
bank.why: Competitiveness and drive.
bank.xq: Type A people are highly competitive, impatient and driven to achieve, and they tend to treat everything as a contest. Which of the following quotations best represents the Type A personality?

dw.“Don't worry, be happy.”: That is relaxed Type B thinking.
dw.“Do unto others as you would have them d: That is the golden rule, not competitiveness.
dw.“All for one and one for all.”: That is a group-first motto, not competitiveness.

bank.q: Compared with Type B people of equal intelligence, Type A people
bank.a: earn more but are less satisfied with themselves
d: earn less money but are happier with their lives
show lower blood pressure when under stress
delegate work to others more easily
bank.why: They keep striving for more and more.
dh: earn more and are more satisfied with themselves
earn less and are less satisfied with themselves
earn less but are more satisfied with themselves
bank.xq: Researchers compared Type A and Type B people who were matched for intelligence and looked at both their success at work and how they felt about themselves. Compared with Type B people of equal intelligence, Type A people

dw.earn less money but are happier with the: Type A people tend to earn more, but they are not happier.
dw.show lower blood pressure when under str: Type A people show higher blood pressure under stress.
dw.delegate work to others more easily: Type A people delegate less easily.

bank.q: Moderators of stress include all of the following EXCEPT
bank.a: pretending that stressors do not exist
d: psychological hardiness and commitment
a sense of humor about the stressor
predictability and a sense of control
bank.why: Moderators: self-efficacy expectations, hardiness, humor, predictability and control, emotional support.
bank.xq: Some psychological factors can soften the impact of stress, so that two people facing the same stressor are affected very differently. Which of the following is NOT one of these moderators of stress?

dw.a sense of humor about the stressor: A sense of humor is a moderator.

bank.q: What are self-efficacy expectations?
bank.a: Beliefs that our own efforts can bring about desired changes
d: Believing that one has control over one's own life
Beliefs that blow negative events out of proportion
Feedback from others about how one is doing
bank.why: “The little engine that could.” High self-efficacy helps us withstand stress.
dh: Beliefs that others' efforts can bring about desired changes for us
Beliefs that our own efforts cannot change outcomes
Beliefs that luck and fate bring about desired changes
bank.xq: Two nurses are facing the same heavy workload. One believes, "If I organize my time, I can handle this," while the other believes nothing she does will help. In the study of stress, which statement describes the first nurse's beliefs?

dw.Believing that one has control over one': That is internal locus of control, or the control part of hardiness.

bank.q: In Bandura's study, people with high self-efficacy facing feared objects had
bank.a: lower levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline
d: higher levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline
no change in hormone levels
more cortisol and less endorphin
bank.why: They have biological as well as psychological reasons to stay calmer.
dh: higher levels of adrenaline and noradrenaline
lower levels of adrenaline but higher noradrenaline
higher levels of adrenaline but lower noradrenaline
bank.xq: In a study by Albert Bandura, people who were afraid of certain objects were exposed to them, and their stress hormones were measured. Compared with others, the people with high self-efficacy facing the feared objects had

dw.higher levels of adrenaline and noradren: The opposite: high self-efficacy meant lower levels.
dw.more cortisol and less endorphin: The study measured adrenaline and noradrenaline, and they went down.

bank.q: Psychological hardiness consists of which three characteristics?
bank.a: Commitment, challenge and control
d: Expectations, humor and control
Power, control and commitment
Confidence, competence and efficacy
bank.why: From Suzanne Kobasa's research on business executives who resisted illness despite stress.
dh: Commitment, competence and control
Confidence, challenge and control
Commitment, challenge and calmness
bank.xq: Research on business executives found that some stayed healthy even under heavy stress, and these executives shared a set of three characteristics called psychological hardiness. Which three characteristics make up psychological hardiness?

dw.Expectations, humor and control: Expectations and humor are separate moderators, not parts of hardiness.
dw.Power, control and commitment: Power is not one of the three: they are commitment, challenge and control.
dw.Confidence, competence and efficacy: Confidence, competence and efficacy are not the three.

bank.q: Our understanding of psychological hardiness comes mainly from whose work?
bank.a: Suzanne Kobasa
d: Julian Rotter
Hans Selye
Shelley Taylor
bank.why: She studied executives who stayed healthy despite stress.
bank.xq: Studies of executives who remained healthy under great stress led to the concept of psychological hardiness, a set of traits that buffer the effects of stress. Our understanding of psychological hardiness comes mainly from whose work?

dw.Julian Rotter: Julian Rotter proposed locus of control.

bank.q: In psychological hardiness, what is commitment?
bank.a: Involving oneself in what one is doing rather than feeling alienated from it
d: Seeing change, rather than stability, as normal and as a chance to grow
Believing that one has control over one's own life
Believing that one can accomplish a certain task
bank.why: Hardy executives involved themselves in what they were doing.
dh: Feeling alienated from what one is doing rather than involved in it
Seeing what one is doing as a chance to grow rather than a threat
Believing one controls what one is doing rather than outside forces
bank.xq: A nurse throws herself into her work, feels that what she does matters, and cares about her patients, rather than feeling that her job means nothing to her. In psychological hardiness, which statement describes this component, called commitment?

bank.q: In psychological hardiness, what is challenge?
bank.a: Seeing change, rather than stability, as normal and as a chance to grow
d: Involving oneself in what one is doing rather than feeling alienated from it
Believing that one has control over one's own life
Seeking social contact and support under stress
bank.why: Hardy people see change as an incentive to grow, not a threat.
dh: Seeing stability, rather than change, as normal and as a chance to grow
Seeing change, rather than stability, as a threat to be avoided
Involving oneself in change rather than feeling alienated from it
bank.xq: When his hospital introduces a new system, one employee sees it as a normal part of life and a chance to learn something new, rather than a threat to his comfortable routine. In psychological hardiness, which statement describes this component, called challenge?
